title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
萬曆五年會試錄

資善大夫禮部尚書兼翰林院學士馬自强〔體乾陝西同州人癸丑進士〕

translation_en:
Record of the Metropolitan Examination of the Fifth Year of the Wanli Reign (1577)

Administrators of the Tribute Examination (知貢舉官):
Ma Ziqiang 馬自强 (courtesy name Tiqian 體乾, a native of Tongzhou, Shaanxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the guichou year [1553]), Grand Master for Assisting toward Goodness, Minister of Rites, and concurrently Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy.
Wang Tang 汪鏜 (courtesy name Zhenzong 振宗, a native of Yin County, Zhejiang, and a metropolitan graduate of the dingwei year [1547]), Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Left Vice Minister of Rites, and concurrently Academician Reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy.

Examiners (考試官):
Zhang Siwei 張四維 (courtesy name Ziwei 子維, a native of Puzhou, Shanxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the guichou year [1553]), Grand Master for Assisting toward Goodness, Minister of Rites, and concurrently Grand Secretary of the East Hall.
Shen Shixing 申時行 (courtesy name Rumo 汝默, registered in Wu County, Zhili, originally from Changzhou County, and a metropolitan graduate of the renxu year [1562]), Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Academician Reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy, in charge of the affairs of the Academy.

Associate Examiners (同考試官):
Chen Jingbang 陳經邦 (courtesy name Gongwang 公望, a native of Putian County, Fujian, and a metropolitan graduate of the yichou year [1565]), Left Admonisher of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy.
Chen Siyu 陳思育 (courtesy name Renfu 仁甫, a native of Wuling County, Huguang, and a metropolitan graduate of the yichou year [1565]), Right Approver of the Right Secretariat of the Heir Apparent and concurrently Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy.
Zhu Geng 朱賡 (courtesy name Shaoqin 少欽, a native of Shanyin County, Zhejiang, and a metropolitan graduate of the wuchen year [1568]), Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Fostering Service.
Li Changchun 李長春 (courtesy name Yuanfu 元甫, registered in Fushun County, Sichuan, originally from Gong'an County, Huguang, and a metropolitan graduate of the wuchen year [1568]), Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Fostering Service.
Huang Fengxiang 黃鳳翔 (courtesy name Mingzhou 鳴周, a native of Jinjiang County, Fujian, and a metropolitan graduate of the wuchen year [1568]), Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for-Literae.
Fan Qian 范謙 (courtesy name Ruyi 汝益, a native of Fengcheng County, Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the wuchen year [1568]), Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Attendance.
Liu Jian 劉瑊 (courtesy name Zihuan 子瓛, registered in the Suzhou Guard, Zhili, originally from Xiajiang County, Jiangxi, and a metropolitan graduate of the xinwei year [1571]), Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for-Literae.
Gong Jiachen 公家臣 (courtesy name Gongfu 共甫, a native of Mengyin County, Shandong, and a metropolitan graduate of the xinwei year [1571]), Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for-Literae.
Wang Honghui 王弘誨 (courtesy name Shaochuan 紹傳, a native of Ding'an County, Guangdong, and a metropolitan graduate of the yichou year [1565]), Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Summoned Service.
Wang Zudi 王祖嫡 (courtesy name Yinchang 胤昌, holding officer's registration in the Xinyang Guard, Henan, originally from Dezhou, Shandong, and a metropolitan graduate of the xinwei year [1571]), Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy and Gentleman for Summoned Service.

Chen Sanmo 陳三謨, Gentleman for Fostering Literature and Chief Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel [style name Ruming 汝明, of Renhe County, Zhejiang; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the yichou year (1565)].
Li Dai 李戴, Gentleman for Fostering Literature and Chief Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Rites [style name Renfu 仁夫, of Yanjin County, Henan; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the wuchen year (1568)].
Lin Jingyang 林景暘, Gentleman for Meritorious Achievement and Left Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for War [style name Shaoxi 紹熙, registered in Huating County, Southern Metropolitan Area, originally from Shanghai County; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the wuchen year (1568)].
Wu Yuyan 吳與言, Grand Master for Upright Service and Vice Director acting as Director of the Bureau of Operations in the Ministry of War [style name Zhimu 志黙, of Dabu County, Guangdong; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the yichou year (1565)].
Xu Yuantai 徐元太, Gentleman for Fostering Virtue and Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Honors in the Ministry of Personnel [style name Ruxian 汝賢, of Xuancheng County, Southern Metropolitan Area; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the yichou year (1565)].
Wu Xiu 吳秀, Gentleman for Fostering Uprightness and Secretary of the Huguang Bureau in the Ministry of Justice [style name Yuexian 越賢, registered in Wucheng County, Zhejiang, originally from Wujiang County, Southern Metropolitan Area; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the xinwei year (1571)].

Guo Zhuang 郭莊, Gentleman for Fostering Literature and Investigating Censor of the Shandong Circuit [style name Zili 子蒞, of Huizhou, Shaanxi; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the wuchen year (1568)].

Cao Gao 曹誥, Gentleman for Fostering Uprightness and Secretary of the Bureau of Ceremonies in the Ministry of Rites [style name Zhongxuan 仲宣, of Xiuning County, Southern Metropolitan Area; a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the xinwei year (1571)].

translation_en:
First Session
The Four Books

"Zigong asked: 'What must a man be like so that he may be called an officer-scholar (shi 士)?' The Master said: 'In conducting himself he maintains a sense of shame, and when sent to the four quarters of the world he does not disgrace his ruler's commission—such a man may be called an officer-scholar.' Zigong said: 'I venture to ask about the next in order.' The Master said: 'His clan praises his filial piety, and his neighbors and fellow villagers praise his brotherly respect.' Zigong said: 'I venture to ask about the next in order.' The Master said: 'In his words he insists on trustworthiness, and in his actions he insists on resolute results. What a stubborn little man he is! Yet he may still be considered the next in order.'" [Analects 13.20]

Lu Kejiao 陸可教
Comment by Associate Examiner Acting Vice Director Xu 徐: Concise, clear, elegant, and vigorous—a piece of writing that restores antiquity.
Comment by Associate Examiner Examining Editor Wang 王: It grasps the meaning of the Master's reply to Zigong, and its diction is moreover classically elegant and worthy of serving as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Junior Compiler Gong 公: Concise, pure, clear, and fluent; it ought to be recorded to serve as a model for the multitude of scholars.
Comment by Associate Examiner Junior Compiler Liu 劉: Upright, grand, and conforming to classical standards; the idea of substance prevailing uniquely reveals the fundamental purport.
Comment by Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Zhu 朱: It brings out the Sage's intention of emphasizing the fundamental, clearly and incisively, well worth reciting.
Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Shen 申: Dignified, elegant, precise, and fitting.
Comment by Examiner Grand Secretary Zhang 張: Clear and exact.

When the sage and the worthy graded the ranks of officer-scholars as three, in all of them they sought only that substance should prevail. For that by which an officer-scholar [is valued is?] substance; although their ranks are three, in summary their striving for substance to prevail is the same. Is it not…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
聖賢詳第以示人與且學始乎爲士非獨以名
也其異於齊民必有實焉故子貢有何如斯可
謂士之問蓋欲審所尚耳夫子語之若曰士以
守身爲本學不爲己非士也必也行己有恥乎
士以適用爲賢才不通方非士也必也使四方
不辱君命乎非仁非義之事雖小不爲而豫內
者有實體講信脩睦之猷無往不效而利外者
有實用士必如是而後無忝於稱名也已然此
天下士也不易能也故子貢請問其次子告之
===
===
曰士貴惇倫必自親長始之誠使事親孝宗族
稱焉事長弟鄉黨稱焉肫肫乎順德之孚矣雖
材藝未周要不失爲脩實行者以是語士非其
次乎夫此一鄉士也士未必盡然也故子貢又
問其次子告之曰士貴有恒每於言行徵之誠
使言必期可復焉行必期致决焉硜硜然小人
之度也雖執德未弘要不失爲存實心者以是
語士又非其次乎吁此一節士也士之品其區
別有如此者惟其實勝故與凡民異爾抑子貢

punctuated: 聖賢詳第以示人與？且學始乎爲士，非獨以名也，其異於齊民必有實焉。故子貢有「何如斯可謂士」之問，蓋欲審所尚耳。夫子語之若曰：士以守身爲本，學不爲己，非士也，必也行己有恥乎！士以適用爲賢，才不通方，非士也，必也使四方不辱君命乎！非仁非義之事，雖小不爲，而豫內者有實體；講信脩睦之猷，無往不效，而利外者有實用。士必如是，而後無忝於稱名也已。然此天下士也，不易能也，故子貢請問其次。子告之曰：士貴惇倫，必自親長始之。誠使事親孝，宗族稱焉；事長弟，鄉黨稱焉，肫肫乎順德之孚矣。雖材藝未周，要不失爲脩實行者。以是語士，非其次乎？夫此一鄉士也，士未必盡然也，故子貢又問其次。子告之曰：士貴有恒，每於言行徵之。誠使言必期可復焉，行必期致决焉，硜硜然小人之度也。雖執德未弘，要不失爲存實心者。以是語士，又非其次乎？吁！此一節士也。士之品其區別有如此者，惟其實勝，故與凡民異爾。抑子貢
translation_en:
…the sage and the worthy ranked them in detail to show to people?

Moreover, learning begins with becoming a scholar-official (shi 士), which is not merely a matter of name; what distinguishes him from the common people must lie in substance. Therefore Zigong 子貢 asked, "What must a man be like before he can be called a scholar-official?"—wishing, in truth, to examine what should be esteemed.

The Master spoke to him as if to say: For a scholar-official, guarding one's own person is fundamental; if one's learning is not for oneself, one is no scholar-official—surely he must conduct himself with a sense of shame! For a scholar-official, being fit for practical use is what makes him worthy; if one's talent cannot adapt to all directions, one is no scholar-official—surely, when sent to the four quarters, he must not disgrace his ruler's commission! Matters that are neither humane nor righteous, though small, he will not do, so that what is prepared within has substantial embodiment; plans for cultivating trust and promoting harmony, wherever applied, never fail to prove effective, so that what benefits the outside world has substantial utility. Only when a scholar-official is like this will he bring no shame to the title he bears.

Yet this is a scholar-official of the whole world, which is not easy to achieve; therefore Zigong asked about the next grade. The Master told him: A scholar-official values thickness in human relations, which must begin with parents and elders. If indeed he serves his parents with filial piety so that his clan praises him, and serves his elders with fraternal respect so that his village praises him, how earnestly sincere is the trust inspired by his compliant virtue! Even if his talents and arts are not all-encompassing, in summary he does not fail to be one who cultivates substantial conduct. Spoken of in these terms, is this not the next grade of scholar-official?

Now this is a scholar-official of a single village, and scholar-officials are not necessarily all even like this; therefore Zigong again asked about the next grade. The Master told him: A scholar-official values constancy, which is always verified in his words and deeds. If indeed in his words he insists they be kept, and in his deeds he insists they be carried through to a decisive conclusion, this is the stubbornly unyielding manner of a lesser man. Even if the virtue he holds to is not broad, in summary he does not fail to be one who preserves a substantial heart. Spoken of in these terms, is this not again the next grade of scholar-official?

Alas! This is a scholar-official of a single point of integrity. That the grades of scholar-officials are distinguished in this way is simply because their substance prevails, and therefore they differ from ordinary people. Yet Zigong…

text:
在聖門稱材辯夫子與語士以行已有耻先之
其所貴於士者有在也及兩言其次雖硜硜有
取焉而不單言才固聖人深意哉噫當時士眩
本末至以仁而不佞爲仲弓病夫子又非獨告
子貢也
子曰回之爲人也擇乎中庸得一善則拳
拳服膺而弗失之矣

translation_en:
…among the Sage’s disciples was renowned for his talent and eloquence. When the Master spoke with him about the scholar-official, he placed “conducting oneself with a sense of shame” first, showing where what he valued in a scholar-official truly lay. And when he twice spoke of the next best, even taking something from the stubbornly petty man without speaking merely of talent—truly, this was the Sage’s profound intention! Alas! At that time scholars confused root and branch, to the point of considering “being humane but lacking glibness” a flaw in Zhonggong; thus the Master was not speaking to Zigong alone.

The Master said: “This is the manner of man that Hui was: he chose the Mean and Constant, and whenever he attained a single good, he clasped it firmly to his breast and never lost it.”
By Feng Mengzhen 馮夢禎.
Associate Examiner Chief Supervising Secretary Chen 陳 comments: Refined, pure, dignified, and elegant; it can serve as a model.

Associate Examiner Left Mentor Chen 陳 comments: The reasoning is refined and the phrasing vigorous; an utterly superb essay on the Doctrine of the Mean.
Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Shen 申 comments: Balanced, upright, and free of superficiality.
Examiner Grand Secretary Zhang 張 comments: Rigorous, upright, refined, and lucid.

The Sage praised the Great Worthy for seeking the Way and attaining it deeply, thereby showing his true knowledge. Indeed, to choose the Mean and Constant and be able to hold fast to it is to have attained it deeply; without Master Yan’s true knowledge, who could do this? Zisi quotes the Master’s words as if to say: As for the virtue of the Mean and Constant, it has a fixed principle but no fixed form, so one must certainly value choosing it; it is difficult to attain and easy to lose, so one must also value holding fast to it. Indeed, for a long time few people have been able to do so; only a man such as Hui…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
明睿而旁通深潜而黙識隨事觀理則知無過
不及之爲妙用而萬變錯陳能無眩乎于是審
察之以盡其詳必欲先明乎善也緣物求心則
知不偏不倚之爲實體而百慮紛起能勿殽乎
于是辨别之以求其當固將允執其中也吾見
理愈析而愈精則必隨所擇而有得焉乃其心
愈存而愈固故能隨所得而無失焉篤行之力
與明辨之功交致雖主善無常而一有契悟卽
其據德之資矣拳拳焉中心藏之何有須臾之
===
離耶深造之學與自得之妙相成蓋進善無窮
而凡有貫通皆其依仁之地矣拳拳然終身由
之豈但朞月之守耶吁顏子之能擇能守如此
此之謂眞知而道所由以明也抑夫子嘗稱回
之仁矣觀其視聽言動隨事而精察之非能擇
乎克已復禮三月不違非能守乎蓋其爲仁乃
所以體中庸也彼知及而仁不能守雖得之必
失之于中庸何有哉故曰苟不至德至道不凝
焉君子欲依乎中庸者亦曰學顏子之所學

punctuated: 明睿而旁通，深潜而黙識。隨事觀理，則知無過不及之爲妙用，而萬變錯陳，能無眩乎？于是審察之以盡其詳，必欲先明乎善也。緣物求心，則知不偏不倚之爲實體，而百慮紛起，能勿殽乎？于是辨别之以求其當，固將允執其中也。吾見理愈析而愈精，則必隨所擇而有得焉；乃其心愈存而愈固，故能隨所得而無失焉。篤行之力與明辨之功交致，雖主善無常，而一有契悟，卽其據德之資矣。拳拳焉中心藏之，何有須臾之離耶？深造之學與自得之妙相成，蓋進善無窮，而凡有貫通，皆其依仁之地矣。拳拳然終身由之，豈但朞月之守耶？吁！顏子之能擇能守如此，此之謂眞知，而道所由以明也。抑夫子嘗稱回之仁矣。觀其視聽言動，隨事而精察之，非能擇乎？克已復禮，三月不違，非能守乎？蓋其爲仁，乃所以體中庸也。彼知及而仁不能守，雖得之必失之，于中庸何有哉？故曰：「苟不至德，至道不凝焉。」君子欲依乎中庸者，亦曰學顏子之所學。
translation_en: …clear-sighted and wise with a comprehensive grasp, deeply immersed and silently comprehending. Observing principle in accordance with affairs, he knew that neither exceeding nor falling short is its wondrous function; yet when ten thousand changes are intricately arrayed, how could one not be dazzled? Thereupon he examined them closely to exhaust their details, determined first to be clear about the good. Seeking the mind through things, he knew that leaning neither to one side nor the other is its real substance; yet when a hundred thoughts arise in profusion, how could one not be confused? Thereupon he discriminated among them to seek what was fitting, resolved indeed to hold fast to the mean. We see that the more principle was analyzed, the more refined it became, so that in whatever he chose he was sure to attain something; and the more his mind was preserved, the firmer it became, so that whatever he attained he was able never to lose. The strength of earnest practice and the effort of clear discrimination were brought to bear together: although taking the good as master has no fixed constancy, once there was a flash of comprehension, that very thing became his resource for holding firmly to virtue. Clasping it tightly and treasuring it in the center of his heart, how could he depart from it even for an instant? Learning that reaches deeply and the wonder of personal realization complemented one another: advancing in goodness without end, wherever he achieved thorough penetration, all of it became the ground upon which he clave to humanity. Clasping it tightly and following it throughout his life, how could this be merely keeping to it for a single month? Ah! Master Yan’s ability to choose and ability to hold fast were such as this—this is what is called true knowledge, and it is whereby the Way is made bright. Moreover, the Master once praised Hui’s humanity. Looking at how in seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting he closely examined each matter as it came, was this not the ability to choose? Overcoming the self and returning to propriety, not departing from humanity for three months, was this not the ability to hold fast? Indeed, his practice of humanity was the very means by which he embodied the Mean. As for those whose knowledge reaches it but whose humanity cannot keep it, even though they attain it they will surely lose it—what have they to do with the Mean? Therefore it is said: “Unless there is supreme virtue, the supreme Way cannot be crystallized.” The gentleman who wishes to cleave to the Mean should simply say: learn what Master Yan learned.

"I too wish to rectify men's hearts, put an end to perverse doctrines, oppose one-sided actions, and banish licentious expressions, so as to carry on the work of the three sages. Do I take pleasure in disputing? I have no choice."

Because the great worthy took the moral instruction of the world as his own responsibility, his discourse refuting perverse doctrines was detailed. Grave indeed is the harm that perverse doctrines do to men's hearts! Succeeding the three sages and taking up the responsibility for the moral instruction of the world, how could Mencius not refute them in detail? In his repeated explanation to Gongduzi 公都子, it was as if he said: Quelling disorder depends on men, and illuminating the Way is done through words. As for Yu 禹, the Duke of Zhou 周, and Confucius 孔子, in turning disorder into order, their respective ages surely depended on each of them. Now, however, Yang Zhu 楊朱 and Mo Di 墨翟 engage in unbridled discussions, benevolence and righteousness are blocked up, and the obscurity of the Way is extreme; men's hearts are drowned in error, one-sidedness and licentiousness arise together, and the disorder of the world has reached its limit. Now that the three sages have passed away, the task of illuminating the Way and awakening the people so as to return the world to order is solely my responsibility. Therefore, I too wish to rectify men's hearts and put an end to perverse doctrines, to oppose one-sided actions and banish licentious expressions. By holding up benevolence [and righteousness?]…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
一本原而於無父無君之敎則遏之期于經
正民興以纉平寧之績蓋嘗深切著明其說矣
而非好也究離道之末流而於害政害事之弊
則防之期於撥亂反正以繼春秋之志蓋嘗丁
寧反復其言矣而非好也人心之蔽錮已深則
提撕之不容于不力雖盡吾辭猶懼道之不□
無以臻廓如之效也欲相忘於無言得乎邪□
之橫流方熾則詆斥之不容于不嚴雖竭吾力
猶懼勢之莫反無能破執一之非也欲置之於
===
不論得乎吁此予說之所以長也世運民生將
於是賴焉外人烏知予之心哉抑孟子時百家
之說眾矣獨辯楊墨何也天下之道邪不能干
正而似常足亂真楊墨之言仁義蓋其似哉故
孟子懼其亂真也噫後世道術之裂久矣學孔
孟者其無使似之亂真哉
易
象曰天行健君子以自彊不息
陸可敎

punctuated:
一本原，而於無父無君之敎則遏之，期于經正民興，以纉平寧之績，蓋嘗深切著明其說矣，而非好也；究離道之末流，而於害政害事之弊則防之，期於撥亂反正，以繼《春秋》之志，蓋嘗丁寧反復其言矣，而非好也。人心之蔽錮已深，則提撕之不容于不力，雖盡吾辭，猶懼道之不□，無以臻廓如之效也，欲相忘於無言，得乎？邪□之橫流方熾，則詆斥之不容于不嚴，雖竭吾力，猶懼勢之莫反，無能破執一之非也，欲置之於不論，得乎？吁！此予說之所以長也。世運民生，將於是賴焉，外人烏知予之心哉？抑孟子時，百家之說眾矣，獨辯楊、墨，何也？天下之道，邪不能干正，而似常足亂真。楊、墨之言仁義，蓋其似哉！故孟子懼其亂真也。噫！後世道術之裂久矣，學孔、孟者，其無使似之亂真哉！
易
象曰：「天行健，君子以自彊不息。」

translation_en:
… [reveal the] fundamental source [of benevolence and righteousness?], and as for the teachings that deny father and ruler, I suppress them, hoping that the constant norms will be rectified and the common people aroused to goodness, so as to continue the achievements of bringing peace and tranquility; indeed, I have explained my arguments deeply, incisively, and clearly, yet not out of fondness for disputing! I trace the degenerate streams that depart from the Way, and as for the abuses that harm governance and affairs, I guard against them, hoping to quell chaos and return to orthodoxy, so as to carry on the aim of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu); indeed, I have repeated my words with earnest care, yet not out of fondness for disputing! When the obscuration and obstinacy of human minds have already become deep, awakening them cannot but be vigorous; even if I exhaust my words, I still fear that the Way will not [be manifest?] and that there will be no means to achieve the effect of sweeping clarity—should I wish to forget myself in silence, would that be possible? When the rampant flood of heterodox [doctrines?] is just ablaze, denouncing and repulsing them cannot but be strict; even if I exhaust my strength, I still fear that the trend cannot be reversed and that I will be unable to shatter the fallacy of clinging to a single extreme—should I wish to set them aside without discussion, would that be possible? Alas! This is why my explanations are so lengthy. The destiny of the age and the livelihood of the people shall depend upon this; how could outsiders know my heart? Yet in Mencius's time, the doctrines of the Hundred Schools were numerous; why did he dispute only Yang Zhu and Mo Di? Among the ways of the world, the heterodox cannot encroach upon the orthodox, yet what merely resembles the truth is always sufficient to confound the genuine. When Yang and Mo spoke of benevolence and righteousness, theirs was indeed a semblance of them! Therefore Mencius feared that they would confound the genuine. Alas! In later ages, the fracturing of the Way and its methods has gone on for a long time; may those who study Confucius and Mencius never allow what merely resembles the truth to confound the genuine!

Book of Changes (Yi)

"The Image says: 'The movement of Heaven is full of power; thus the superior man makes himself strong and untiring.'"

《彖傳》明乾義，天有常運，而君子有常心焉。蓋天運而不已，惟其健也；君子之心，純乎天矣，寧不與之同運哉？今夫乾，天也，天下之至健也。上下皆乾，則天之行昭焉。往來相禪，氣常運而不積；闔闢相推，機常轉而不窮，斯其爲至健也已。而君子何以法之？天賦人以德，其健同也，有欲則餒矣；人受健于天，其不息同也，有息非健矣。惟君子純粹以精之德，性而有之，其清明之在躬者，既不淆于氣禀；發强剛毅之操，安而行之，其義理之用事者，復不間于物交。以之制心，則敬勝怠焉，存于無感之先，而一毫之私意不使

The Commentary on the Images [here transcribed as Commentary on the Judgments, Tuanzhuan] clarifies the meaning of the Qian hexagram: Heaven has its constant movement, and the noble man has his constant mind. Indeed, that Heaven moves without cease is solely because of its vigor; since the mind of the noble man is purely aligned with Heaven, how could it not move in unison with it? Now Qian is Heaven, the most vigorous thing under heaven. Both the upper and lower trigrams being Qian, the movement of Heaven is made manifest. Going and coming succeed one another, as vital energy constantly circulates without stagnating; closing and opening impel one another, as the pivotal mechanism constantly revolves without exhaustion—such is its supreme vigor. And how does the noble man emulate it? Heaven endows human beings with virtue, so their vigor is the same, yet when there is selfish desire, it becomes deflated; human beings receive their vigor from Heaven, so their unceasingness is the same, yet when there is cessation, it is no longer vigorous. Only the noble man possesses by nature a virtue that is unmixed and refined, so that the clear luminosity within his person is unclouded by physical endowment; he practices with ease a conduct that is dynamic, strong, firm, and resolute, so that the moral principle governing his actions is uninterrupted by contact with external things. When by this means he regulates his mind, reverence overcomes indolence: it is preserved prior to any external stimulation, and not a hair's breadth of selfish intent is allowed to…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
萌于念慮發動之初内者不出外者不入而泰
宇之寧定浩浩乎與帝天之命相爲周流矣以
之制事則義以勝欲焉伸于萬物之上而一毫
之私欲不使引于酬酢紛紜之際始不見合終
不見離而天德之流行亹亹焉與造化之神相
爲循環矣是健一也在天有常運卽天之不息
在君子有常心卽君子之行健天人合一之妙
盡於乾如此夫抑君子體乾之功寡欲要矣窮
理急焉蓋人心惟危衆欲易汨非日從事於窮
===
理之學則危微之幾莫辨而剛德斯沮矣古之

萌于念慮發動之初，内者不出，外者不入，而泰宇之寧定，浩浩乎與帝天之命相爲周流矣。以之制事，則義以勝欲焉，伸于萬物之上，而一毫之私欲不使引于酬酢紛紜之際，始不見合，終不見離，而天德之流行，亹亹焉與造化之神相爲循環矣。是健一也，在天有常運，卽天之不息；在君子有常心，卽君子之行健。天人合一之妙，盡於乾如此夫！抑君子體乾之功，寡欲要矣，窮理急焉。蓋人心惟危，衆欲易汨，非日從事於窮理之學，則危微之幾莫辨，而剛德斯沮矣。古之聖人所以乘龍御天、首出庶物者，必曰「惟精惟一」，「學有緝熈于光明」，此所以與天爲一也。
「夫易廣矣大矣，以言乎遠則不禦，以言乎邇則靜而正，以言乎天地之間則備矣。夫乾，其靜也專，其動也直，是以大生焉。夫坤，其靜也翕，其動也闢，是以廣生焉。廣大配天地，變通配四時，陰陽之義配日月，易簡之善配至德。」
translation_en:
…sprout at the very inception of thoughts and intentions; what is within does not leak out, what is without does not intrude, and the serene composure of his inner realm flows boundlessly in concert with the mandate of Heaven on high. When he uses it to regulate affairs, righteousness overcomes desire; standing supreme above the myriad things, he allows not a hair's breadth of selfish desire to entice him amid the bustling complexities of social intercourse. In the beginning no deliberate joining is seen, and in the end no separation, while the coursing of heavenly virtue cycles tirelessly in unison with the spirit of creation. This vigor is one and the same: in Heaven it is constant revolution, which is Heaven's unceasingness; in the superior man it is a constant mind, which is the superior man's vigorous conduct. Such is the wondrous unity of Heaven and man, fully realized in Qian! Yet in the superior man's effort to embody Qian, while lessening desires is essential, exhaustively investigating principles is urgent. For the human mind is precarious and easily submerged by the multitude of desires; unless one engages daily in the learning of exhaustively investigating principles, the subtleincipience of the precarious and the微 [subtle] cannot be discerned, and firm virtue is thereby thwarted. Thus the sages of antiquity, by whom the dragons were mounted to drive across the heavens and who rose preeminent above the multitude of things, necessarily spoke of "being discriminating and undivided" and of "learning that has continuous brightness unto illumination"—this is how they became one with Heaven.

"Now the Changes is broad and great! If we speak of what is far, it knows no bounds; if we speak of what is near, it is still and correct; if we speak of the space between Heaven and Earth, it encompasses all. Now Qian: in its stillness it is concentrated, in its movement it is straight; therefore it produces greatly. Now Kun: in its stillness it closes together, in its movement it opens wide; therefore it produces broadly. In breadth and greatness it matches Heaven and Earth; in change and continuity it matches the four seasons; in the meaning of yin and yang it matches the sun and moon; in the goodness of the easy and simple it matches supreme virtue."

《易》理之廣大，本諸造化而無不合焉。夫造化，理之原也。《易》本乎此，而天人咸相配矣，其廣大何如哉？《大傳》意曰：《易》之為書，孰不謂象數之文已也，豈知其有冒天下之道，而蓄之至廣、廓之至大者乎？何者？天下莫非一理，而《易》理無乎不貫。語遠邇，則充之不禦，體之靜正，隨所至而各足焉；語兩間，則上際乎天，下蟠乎地，合萬有而皆備焉。《易》何廣大若是也？蓋乾坤者，《易》理之宗；動靜者，乾坤之機也。由專而直，乾則先坤而大造

The vastness and greatness of the principles of the Changes (Yi 易) are rooted in the creative transformations of nature, and there is nothing with which they do not accord. Now, the creative transformations of nature are the source of principle. Because the Changes is rooted in this, both Heaven and the human realm are matched by it—how vast and great it is! The meaning of the "Great Treatise" (Dazhuan 大傳) is as follows: Regarding the Changes as a book, who would not say that it is merely a text of images and numbers? Yet how could they know that it encompasses the Way of all under Heaven, storing it with the utmost vastness and expanding it to the utmost greatness? Why is this? Everything under Heaven is nothing other than a single principle, and there is nothing that the principle of the Changes does not penetrate. Speaking of what is distant and what is near, when extended it cannot be stopped, and when embodied it is tranquil and correct—wherever it reaches, it is in each case fully sufficient. Speaking of what is between Heaven and Earth, above it reaches to Heaven and below it coils across the Earth, bringing together the myriad things so that all are complete within it. Why is the Changes as vast and great as this? It is because Qian 乾 and Kun 坤 are the foundation of the principles of the Changes, and movement and stillness are the pivotal mechanisms of Qian and Kun. 乎羣生，易觀象於乾，大以生矣；由翕而闢，坤則後乾而廣育乎庶類，易觀法於坤，廣以生矣。惟廣大生於乾坤，故其大也，萬象兼該，與天之昆侖無外者準焉；其廣也，百物具舉，與地之旁礴無疆者竝焉。廣大之化裁者，變通之機也，而天地之四時，亦以變通錯行，易相為參矣；廣大之分布者，陰陽之義也，而天地之日月，亦以陰陽懸象，易相為昭矣；廣大有易簡之善，言乎健順者也，而人心之至德，一天地健順之理焉，易相為流通也。蓋所謂遠邇、兩間悉備者，皆是物也。廣矣大矣，其弗信乎？抑以見聖心之廣大也。聖人成位乎乾坤，其大生、廣生之理，皆其心所統會者。以此心作之易，則易豈屑屑象數耶？故曰：「聖人立象以盡意。」夫意何所紀極也？彼九師、五子之說，徒徇其象而不求其意，斯隘矣。

translation_en:
…all living beings; the Book of Changes (Yi) observes its images in Qian, and from this its greatness is generated. From closing in stillness to opening in movement, Kun follows after Qian and broadly nurtures all the myriad categories of things; the Book of Changes observes its models in Kun, and from this its breadth is generated. Because its breadth and greatness are generated from Qian and Kun, in its greatness it encompasses all phenomena, matching the all-encompassing boundlessness of Heaven; in its breadth it brings forth the hundred things in their entirety, standing alongside the vast and limitless expanse of Earth. The transformation and regulation within its breadth and greatness are the pivot of change and continuity; and as the four seasons of Heaven and Earth likewise alternate and proceed through change and continuity, the Book of Changes forms a triad with them. The distribution within its breadth and greatness is the principle of yin and yang; and as the sun and moon of Heaven and Earth likewise suspend their images through yin and yang, the Book of Changes shines in concert with them. Its breadth and greatness possess the goodness of ease and simplicity, which speaks to vigor and順 compliance; and the supreme virtue of the human mind is one with the principle of vigor and compliance of Heaven and Earth, with which the Book of Changes flows in mutual communion. Indeed, what was referred to as being fully present whether far or near and throughout the space between Heaven and Earth is none other than this. Vast indeed, great indeed—how could one not believe it?

Moreover, by this we may see the breadth and greatness of the sage's mind. The sage establishes his position between Qian and Kun, and the principles of great generation and broad generation are all unified and gathered within his mind. Having composed the Book of Changes with this mind, how could the Book of Changes be merely preoccupied with trivial images and numbers? Thus it is said: "The sages established the images in order to express their meaning fully." And what limit or end can there be to that meaning? Those doctrines of the Nine Masters (Jiushi) and the Five Masters (Wuzi), which merely cling to its images without seeking its meaning, are narrow indeed!

When the great minister recounts in sequence the difficulties of inaugurating an era of peace and prosperity, it is thereby to lodge deeply the intention of preserving that peace and prosperity. Now, with the people at peace and governance in order, Yu 禹 had opened up great peace for ten thousand generations, yet bringing it about was exceedingly difficult; that he should work tirelessly to preserve it was certainly fitting. Imagine his reply to Gao Yao 皐陶, as if to say: "In governance, nothing is more valuable than planning for the end, while peace and security are always hardest at the very beginning. When I think of working tirelessly day after day, how could it be without reason? For in the past, when the floodwaters were not yet pacified, the harm they caused to the myriad states and the multitudes of the people was extreme. Only I bore the responsibility of controlling the waters, and Yi 益 and Ji 稷 truly assisted me. At first, because the perils of the waters were bound up with the mountains, I rode in the four conveyances to survey what was suitable, and followed the nine mountain ranges to hew away their obstructions, so that earthworks could begin. At that time I went forth together with Yi, and to the people who were distressed by hunger we first bequeathed the benefit of fresh meat and fish. And yet this was not all. text:

以播而衆之艱於食者不廢夫鮮食之奏焉而

遂懋勉夫斯民予之所以拯溺亨屯除害興利

海，濬畎澮以歸之川，而田功可興矣。時則曁稷以播，而衆之艱於食者，不廢夫鮮食之奏焉，而猶未也。山澤之利，旣漸積於天下，而有無之易，遂懋勉夫斯民。予之所以拯溺亨屯、除害興利者，至是不遺餘力矣。夫然後天地底於平成，府事臻於脩治。觀諸烝民，始熈熈然粒食焉，非復艱食之歎也；觀諸萬邦，始蒸蒸其作乂焉，非復俾乂之憂也。蓋躬之以八年之勤，濟之以二臣之力，成功若此其難也，而孜孜其可忘邪？雖然，禹之言若嫌於屑屑自言功矣，不知述艱難之業，正以動儆戒之思，大臣爲國家長遠慮固如此。不然，不矜不伐之稱，豈虛也哉？卒之鞀韶竝設，典則俱垂，而其孜孜之心益見矣。蓋孔子無間然於禹，於乎，諒哉！

translation_en:
… the sea, and dredged the field channels and ditches to guide them into the rivers, so that farming work could be raised up. At that time, together with Ji I sowed the grain, and for the multitudes who found it hard to get food, we did not neglect to present them with fresh meats from the waters; and yet that was still not all. Once the benefits of mountains and marshes had gradually accumulated throughout the realm, we urged the people to exchange what they had for what they lacked. In rescuing the drowning and bringing relief from distress, in removing harm and promoting benefit, I had by this point spared no effort. Only then were Heaven and Earth brought to order and completion, and the six treasuries and three governance affairs brought to a state of well-regulated repair. Looking at the multitude of people, they finally enjoyed grain food in happy harmony, no longer lamenting the hardship of finding food; looking at the myriad states, they finally rose up in flourishing order, no longer giving cause for anxiety over how to bring them under governance. Indeed, having personally devoted eight years of toil to it, aided by the strength of those two ministers, achieving success was as difficult as this—how then could unremitting diligence be forgotten?

Even so, Yu's words might seem open to the suspicion of pettily recounting his own merits. Yet people do not realize that his recounting of this arduous enterprise was precisely meant to stir thoughts of caution and vigilance; such is naturally the far-sighted concern of a great minister for the state. Otherwise, how could his reputation for neither boasting nor bragging have been empty? In the end, when the hand-drum and bell were set out together and his canons and rules were handed down for posterity, his unremittingly diligent heart became all the more evident. Truly, when Confucius found no flaw in Yu—ah, how well-founded that was!

"In governance, value constancy; in pronouncements, prize substance and conciseness."
By Shen Zibin 沈自邠.

Associate Examiner Chen, Right Admonisher, comments: "Concise in wording and clear in meaning; worthy of being recorded as a model."

賢王示政令所當崇者而治體備矣夫爲治有
大體也政有恒則民易守辭體要則民易信于
致治乎何有康王舉以告畢公若曰化民成俗
者非立治功之爲難而敦治體之爲急公之保
釐東郊也是在識體而已彼旌淑别慝布之章
===

恒久之規則紛更多事豈惟民無所適從而于

持不易之法經制既定久道以俟之可也典常

賢王示政令所當崇者，而治體備矣。夫爲治有大體也。政有恒則民易守，辭體要則民易信，于致治乎何有？康王舉以告畢公，若曰：化民成俗者，非立治功之爲難，而敦治體之爲急。公之保釐東郊也，是在識體而已。彼旌淑别慝，布之章程，則爲政。政者，整齊斯民，與之共守者也。上無恒久之規，則紛更多事，豈惟民無所適從，而于施政之體亦褻矣。必也貴有恒焉。以無倦之心，持不易之法，經制既定，久道以俟之可也；典常是師，畫一而守之可也。雖由俗之政不嫌于變通，然深計遠謀，納殷民于寧一之化者，莫善于此，斯其爲可貴乎！彰善癉惡，敷之號令，則爲辭。辭者，訓導斯民，俾之承聽者也。上無典重之言，則浮華失實，匪惟民無所取信，而于出令之體
translation_en:
Associate Examiner and Left Admonisher Chen comments: [Classic and elegant without superficiality; these too are words of substance and concision, fit to serve as a model for the multitude of scholars.]
Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting Shen comments: [Concise, substantial, and illuminating.]
Examiner and Grand Secretary Zhang comments: [Gentle, profound, and refined.]

When the worthy king points out what ought to be esteemed in administrative measures and ordinances, the fundamentals of governance are complete. Now, governing has its great fundamentals. When governance has constancy, the people find it easy to abide by; when words have substance and concision, the people find them easy to trust—what difficulty, then, is there in achieving good order? King Kang raised this to instruct the Duke of Bi, as if to say: In transforming the people and perfecting customs, it is not establishing administrative achievements that is difficult, but rather earnestly attending to the fundamentals of governance that is urgent. In Your Grace's pacifying and ordering of the eastern suburbs, everything lies simply in recognizing the fundamentals.

Now, distinguishing the good and separating out the evil, and promulgating this in statutes and regulations—that is governance. Governance is that by which one brings order to the people and upholds standards together with them. If those above lack enduring rules, there will be chaotic alterations and meddlesome affairs; not only will the people have nothing to follow, but the very dignity of administering governance will also be profaned. One must, of necessity, value constancy! With an untiring mind, maintain unchangeable laws: once the institutional framework is settled, one may bide one's time through a lasting Way; taking constant norms as one's model, one may preserve them with uniformity. Although governance that accommodates local customs does not shy away from flexible adaptation, when it comes to deep plans and far-sighted counsels for bringing the people of Yin into a tranquil and unified transformation, nothing is better than this—is this not why it is to be valued?

Manifesting the good and chastising the wicked, and setting this forth in proclamations and ordinances—that is words. Words are that by which one instructs and guides the people so as to make them heed and obey. If those above lack grave and canonical speech, there will be flashy extravagance and a loss of substance; not only will the people have nothing in which to place their trust, but the very dignity of issuing ordinances…

translation_en:
… is also frivolous. Rather, one must surely esteem what is essential and concise: using principles that are easy and simple to utter words that are profound and substantial. In the guidance provided by constant moral teachings, one aims for their purport to be enduringly meaningful; in the manifestation of virtuous pronouncements, one desires their significance to be precise and succinct. Although moving the people with words does not preclude repetition, when it comes to emphasizing fundamentals, esteeming substance, and returning the people of Yin to honest and simple customs, nothing is more urgent than this—is this not what ought to be esteemed? Now, when governance has constancy, the people will all comply with governance; when pronouncements are essential and concise, the people will all be transformed by instruction. Otherwise, who could rescue the degenerate customs of Shang? This is why the responsibility of protecting and regulating was so deeply hoped for in the Duke of Bi (Bi Gong 畢公). Alas! Were the words of King Kang (Kang Wang 康王) meant only to rescue the degenerate customs of Shang? Indeed, the essentials of governance are complete in them. Those arguments for disruptive change merely throw old statutes into confusion, and華麗 (extravagant and ornate) rhetoric brings no benefit to practical use—what reliance can the state place upon them? Confucius said, "Abide in it without weariness," which speaks of having constancy; he said, "In words, it is enough that they convey the meaning," which speaks of being essential and concise. Was he not thinking of rescuing the decline of the Way of Zhou? Thus, the words of King Kang are truly a model for ten thousand generations.

"The skins of the lambs and sheep, with five braidings of white silk. They retire for their meal from the court, self-possessed and easy, self-possessed and easy."

服有常而容自得，南國之大夫然也。蓋節儉故其服有常，正直故其容自得也。南國大夫以之，文王之化可徵矣。詩人述而美之，若謂：君子敦朴以先民，是故一章服也而人皆趨之，胡可忽也？我大夫安節之亨，裁之法服者無論已，卽私居之服而有羔羊之皮者，吾猶見其素絲五紽焉。絲取於素，昭其質也；紽取於五，昭其度也。蓋不必玄黃黼黻以為觀，而冲然有君子之服矣。此非節儉之存而為共德也，其章之服御有是哉？君子正色以率下，是故一動容也而人皆仰之，胡可苟也？我大夫元吉之旋，形之公朝者無論已，卽退食之時而從公門以出也，吾猶見其委蛇委蛇焉。神怡於公暇，而雍容之度宣也；情適於退思，而泮奐之休著也。蓋不必采齊肆夏…

Associate Examiner and Junior Compiler Fan comments: Solemn and purely elegant, amply possessing the bearing of a minister of Zhou.
Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Li comments: Placid and effortless, like the sweeping sound of courtly music!
Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting Shen comments: Pure and refined, worthy of appreciation.
Examiner and Grand Secretary Zhang comments: Brisk and fluent.

Their dress follows constant norms and their demeanor is self-possessed—such were the grandees of the southern states. Because they were frugal, their dress followed constant norms; because they were upright, their demeanor was self-possessed. That the grandees of the southern states were so is proof of the transforming influence of King Wen. The poet recounted and praised this, as if to say: The superior man leads the people through honest simplicity; therefore, even in a single item of patterned attire, everyone follows his example—how could it be treated lightly? Our grandees enjoy the success of contentedly keeping to proper bounds. Not to speak of what is tailored for their statutory court robes, even in the garments of their private residence made of lambskin, we still see them braided with五 (five) braids of white silk. The silk is chosen to be white to manifest its unadorned substance; the braids are set at five to manifest proper measure. Indeed, there is no need for black and yellow or embroidered axe-patterns to make a display, and yet in modest simplicity they possess the attire of a superior man. Were it not that frugality is preserved within them as a shared virtue, how could its manifestation in their dress and equipage be like this? The superior man rectifies his countenance to lead his subordinates; therefore, in a single movement or expression, everyone looks up to him—how could he be careless? Our grandees, in the auspiciousness of their conduct, not to speak of how it is manifested at the public court, even when they retire for their meals and emerge from the court gates, we still see them moving with easy, self-possessed grace. Their spirit is serene in their leisure from public duty, and a poised and dignified bearing is displayed; their feelings are at ease as they retire for reflection, and a relaxed and unhurried excellence is made evident. Indeed, there is no need for the strains of the Caiqi and Sixia airs…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
以為趨而坦然有君子之容矣此非正直之宅
而無愧心也其施諸容體有是哉要之皆文王
卑服之節敬止之範先之噫吾於是而知聖化
之入人深矣大抵國家之敗由官邪也官之失
德寵賂章也故節儉者常正直而正直者未有
不節儉周之興也有素絲委蛇之歌比其衰也
則有維鵜相鼠之刺是故一容一服之間而觀
風化者常先焉治天下者可以審所尚矣
其胤維何天被爾祿君子萬年景命有僕

以為趨，而坦然有君子之容矣。此非正直之宅，而無愧心也，其施諸容體有是哉？要之，皆文王卑服之節、敬止之範先之。噫！吾於是而知聖化之入人深矣。大抵國家之敗，由官邪也；官之失德，寵賂章也。故節儉者常正直，而正直者未有不節儉。周之興也，有《素絲》委蛇之歌；比其衰也，則有《維鵜》、《相鼠》之刺。是故一容一服之間，而觀風化者常先焉，治天下者可以審所尚矣。

「其胤維何？天被爾祿。君子萬年，景命有僕。其僕維何？釐爾女士。釐爾女士，從以孫子。」

translation_en:
…to set the pace of his stride, and yet with composed ease he possesses the bearing of a gentleman. Were his mind not the dwelling place of uprightness, free of any cause for shame, could it be manifested in his demeanor and carriage like this? In sum, all of this was led by King Wen's frugality in humble dress and his standard of reverent comportment. Ah! From this I know how deeply the transformative influence of the sage penetrates into men. Generally speaking, the ruin of a state comes from the wickedness of officials, and the officials' loss of virtue comes from the open display of favoritism and bribery. Therefore, those who are frugal are always upright, and there has never been one who is upright without being frugal. When the Zhou rose, there was the song of "white silk" and "self-possessed ease" [in the ode "Lambswool" (Gao yang)]; by the time of its decline, there were the satires of "The Pelican" (Wei ti, i.e., "Pelican on the Dam" [Hou ren]) and "Look at the Rat" (Xiang shu). For this reason, between a single expression of demeanor and a single article of dress, observers of moral customs always look first; those who govern the world may well examine what they esteem.

"What will that posterity be? Heaven covers you with blessings. For the lord, ten thousand years; the great mandate has its attachments. What will those attachments be? It grants you heroic women. It grants you heroic women, and following them, grandsons and sons." [Book of Odes, "Drunk with Wine" (Ji zui)]
By Ye Chengyu 葉承遇.

Associate Examiner Examining Editor Wang comments: Refined, pure, antique, and elegant; skillful at bringing out the poet's intent.
Associate Examiner Historiographer Fan comments: Praising him and ultimately returning to praying to Heaven for an enduring mandate—how loyal!
Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Li comments: Its spirit and flavor are loyal and sincere, expressed with gentle grace.
Examiner Expositor-in-Waiting Shen comments: Neat, clean, and full of engaging flavor.

詩人詳神之錫類于君祚胤相因者也夫子孫
福祿相為憑依者也一開之一繼之神謀不旣
周乎宜父兄歌以答君賜也意曰神之于君其
保佑之也隆故其計安之也備觀于祚胤之相
因而知之矣彼帝王之胤所託以纘基業于萬
世者也非祚則無以藉前休矣今神欲福君之
孫子而先于君身乎萃焉俾之戩穀而誕膺曆
數萬年履元后之尊也迕以繁祉而光撫輿圖

無疆矣萬年之後孫子得享貽燕之庇者不自
今垂之哉帝王之祚所用以流慶澤于萬世者
也非胤則無以綿遺休矣今神欲永君之福祿
而内于孫子乎寄焉命女士以釐降而聖神繼

Examiner Grand Secretary Zhang comments: [Bright, elegant, and conforming to classical standards.]

The poet details how the spirits bestow blessings of kind upon the sovereign, whereby the dynastic fortune and royal posterity mutually depend upon one another. Now, descendants and felicitous blessings rely on each other: one initiates it, the other continues it—are not the designs of the spirits utterly comprehensive? Fitting it is that the royal uncles and elder brothers sing this in reply to the sovereign's bounty.

The meaning is as follows: The spirits, in their regard for the sovereign, protect and aid him abundantly, and therefore their plans for his security are complete; one can know this by observing the mutual dependence of dynastic fortune and royal posterity. 

Those descendants of an emperor or king are the ones entrusted with continuing the foundational enterprise for ten thousand generations; without dynastic fortune, they would have nothing by which to avail themselves of predecessor's blessings. Now the spirits wish to bless the sovereign's grandsons and sons, and so they first gather blessings upon the sovereign's own person: causing him to attain complete goodness and grandly receive the heavenly destiny, occupying the exalted position of supreme ruler for ten thousand years; meeting him [?] with manifold blessings and gloriously pacifying the realm, grasping the weighty sacred vessel of state for ten thousand years. Thus the great mandate attaches to him, and the blessings of the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain are boundless. After ten thousand years, that his grandsons and sons are able to enjoy the shelter of the peace and ease bequeathed to them—is it not handed down from the present?

The dynastic fortune of an emperor or king is that by which auspicious bounty is made to flow down for ten thousand generations; without posterity, there would be nothing by which to prolong the bequeathed blessings. Now the spirits wish to perpetuate the sovereign's felicitous blessings, and so within the palace they entrust this to his grandsons and sons: commanding ladies of virtue to be bestowed in marriage so that sages and divine rulers emerge in succession, the enduring auspice of "the profound opening forth" [of the *Odes*]; selecting fine mates to serve as consorts so that the main line and collateral branches daily proliferate, whereby the hereditary virtues are successfully maintained. Thus his grandsons and sons number in the hundreds of thousands, and the continuation of the great [?] patrimony will never fail. After successive generations, that the sovereign is able to prolong extraordinary grace—is it not joined to him from the present?

Ah! Dynastic fortune precedes posterity as a plan to aid and open the way; posterity succeeds dynastic fortune as…

…as a plan for perpetuating the ancestral legacy, the pure blessing of the One Man is complete. Such is the excellence of bestowing blessings on one's kind! Even so, how could the poet merely be indulging in extravagant praise and prayer? The person of the sovereign is that upon which his descendants rely; moral beneficence and good fortune all originate from oneself. Suppose one does not pray to Heaven for an enduring mandate—on what then can one rely to entrust the state to future generations? Treading in the midst of prosperity and contemplating its preservation, there must be a long-term policy that establishes the foundation for ten thousand generations. The ode "All-delighted" (Jia le) sings: "Illustrious is his admirable virtue; he orders well the common people and the officers." Ah, this is surely what the honoured minister wished to express!

translation_en:
… this action indeed say: "It was merely a subtle expedient to rectify the world; why then censure the four states?" The gentleman says: "The relationship between ruler and subject is the great distinction of status. Ever since Kings Wen and Wu, all under Heaven have revered Zhou as their宗 (suzerain). Although the House of Zhou has declined, the Mandate of Heaven has not changed. All of us in the covenant should rightly make honoring and supporting [the royal house] our concern—what need is there for a hegemon? Now Duke Huan of Qi initiated it, and the four states consequently attached themselves to him. Caps and robes gathered together, unanimously plotting to exalt and support him as leader; did they alone not consider whether the mandate of the battle-axe [to punish on the king's behalf] had actually been received from above or not? Thereafter, those who schemed for hegemony and contended for supremacy followed on one another's heels in the domain of the feudal lords, and the tracks of Eastern Zhou never revived again—thus this meeting was the stepping-stone to ruin. Therefore the Classic demotes them and calls them 'people' (ren), so as to lament that there was no true king in the world."

When Jin and Chu concluded a peace agreement, that was the reason for the blood-covenant at Song. Those who praise this action indeed say: "It was merely a good policy for halting warfare; why then blame the various Great Officers?" The gentleman says: "The boundary between barbarian and Chinese (Yi and Xia) is the great defense. Ever since Dukes Huan [of Qi] and Wen [of Jin], the Central States had ostracized Chu. 'If they are not of our kindred clan, their hearts are surely different.' These friendly states should rightly have taken smiting and punishing [the barbarians] as their watchword—what need was there for a covenant? Now Qu Jian requested it, and Jin along with the various states mistakenly listened to and followed him. Ascending the covenant altar together, they flocked to form friendly relations of mutual audience; did they never consider whether the deceit of armor hidden beneath robes could be relied upon for security or not? Thereafter, envoys holding jade tablets and presenting silk offerings were seen in steady succession on the roads to barbaric Jing (Chu), and the ominous aura of its northern ambitions blazed more fiercely by the day—thus this covenant was the fountainhead of the deluge. Therefore the Classic repeats the phrase 'at Song' to lament that there was no hegemon in the world."

Alas! This meeting and this covenant were both great turning points in the rise and fall of the Way of the world. Once a misstep is made at the beginning, it can no longer be guarded against afterward; …

Yet in the hegemony of Duke Huan of Qi, his nine assemblies and single rectification of the realm were still sufficient to alleviate the threat of falling under barbarian rule ("buttoning robes on the left"); whereas for Jin, once it concluded the single covenant at Song, the achievements of Dukes Wen, Xiang, and Dao were swept away and fell into decline. Chu had besieged Song for a long time. The wrath with which the King of Chu flung his sleeve as he rose was enough to destroy Song, and the envoys sent to plead for urgent aid brought no relief in resisting Chu. punctuated: 元人楚師也，非使之告病於楚也；莊之謀於申叔時也，非遽欲釋宋而去也。今登牀而告，元也私其情於子反焉。彼固謂易子析骸之困，國不可以朝夕，取必於上而請平矣。乗堙而見，反也私其情於華元焉。彼固謂師有七日之糧，勢不可以持久，取必於上而許平矣。故退師之盟，主之者初無成命，而特定於華元之私約；取此而歸，持之者豈無成算，而不能勝子反之一言。是二臣者，使其君舉國而聽之耳。噫！宋有不欺之臣，雖足取重於敵國，而輕見情實，以其國蹈不測之險，將奚以有詞于君？楚有矜厄之義，雖足徼惠于友邦，而攘善君側，以其身冒不可居之功，為之君者不亦難乎？此而不貶，則功可以幸成，而君臣之大倫廢矣。故特貶而人之，以為貪功無上者之戒。蓋《春秋》之義，其嚴如此。抑子反之罪，無庸論已。申舟之釁，元實啟之。身為正卿，不聞有折衝禦侮之猷，而挑釁强夷，幾危社稷，區區之功不足贖矣，矧又專之耶！乃魚石猶稱
translation_en: … [Hua] Yuan to enter [reading 人 as 入] the Chu army, it was not to have him disclose their distress to Chu; and when [King] Zhuang [of Chu] consulted with Shen Shushi, he did not immediately wish to release Song and depart. Yet by climbing onto [Zifan's] couch to tell him, [Hua] Yuan privately shared his true situation with Zifan. Thinking that in the plight of exchanging children to eat and splitting bones for fuel the state could not last from morning to evening, he presumed upon his sovereign's compliance and sued for peace. And by mounting the siege ramp to meet him, [Zi]fan privately shared his true situation with Hua Yuan. Thinking that with only seven days' provisions left for the army the campaign could not be sustained for long, he presumed upon his sovereign's compliance and granted peace. Thus, as for the covenant to withdraw the troops, the ruler presiding over it initially gave no established command, and it was settled solely by Hua Yuan's private pact; and as for accepting this and returning home, how could the ruler holding the reins lack a settled plan, yet he could not prevail over a single word from Zifan. These two ministers simply forced their rulers to hand over the decision for their entire states and obey them! Alas! Though Song had a minister who would not deceive, which was enough to win respect from an enemy state, by lightly revealing the true situation and making his state tread into unfathomable danger, what excuse could he offer to his ruler? And though Chu had the righteousness of pitying those in distress, which was enough to seek favor with a neighboring state, by usurping credit at his ruler's side and personally claiming a merit he had no right to occupy, did he not make it difficult for the one who was his ruler? If this were not censured, then merit could be achieved by luck, and the great moral bond between ruler and minister would be destroyed. Therefore, [the Spring and Autumn Annals] specially censured them by referring to them merely as "men" (ren), as a warning to those who are greedy for merit and have no regard for their superiors. Such is the strictness of the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu). Moreover, Zifan's offense needs no further discussion. As for the feud over Shen Zhou, [Hua] Yuan actually provoked it. Being himself the chief minister, he was never heard to possess any strategy for repelling aggression or defending against insult; instead, he provoked a powerful barbarian state and nearly endangered the altars of soil and grain. His paltry merit was not enough to redeem his fault—how much less when he monopolized it for himself! Yet Yu Shi still praised him, …

君子盡脩己之實，而禮之本立矣。夫禮，不可以虛行也。君子脩其言行，則德無不實矣，謂不有以立禮之本乎？且禮緣人情而作者也，故其用雖散殊於天下，而其本則統會於吾身。行禮者，亦惟反求諸身，加意於言行而已。蓋言者，行之表，行不顧言，非脩也；行者，言之實，言不顧行，非道也。夫固身所不脩，而禮之莫能行也。是以君子學先於自治，而凡擬議之所及者，率履之而不越；功懋於慎脩，而凡話言之所著者，允迪之

"To cultivate one's person and fulfill one's words is called good conduct. When conduct is cultivated and words accord with the Way, that is the substance of ritual."

Shen Jiwen 沈季文

Associate Examiner Acting Director Wu 吳 comments: The reasoning is clear and the phrasing is incisive; it can serve as a model.
Associate Examiner Examining Editor Zhao 趙 comments: Precise and unpretentious; this is writing that returns to substance.
Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Shen 申 comments: Harmoniously integrated and smoothly articulated.
Examiner Grand Secretary Zhang 張 comments: Genuine and incisive.

When the gentleman exhausts the substance of self-cultivation, the foundation of ritual is established. Now, ritual cannot be practiced in vain. When the gentleman cultivates his words and conduct, his virtue is wholly substantive; can it be said that he does not thereby establish the foundation of ritual? Moreover, ritual was created in accordance with human feelings. Therefore, although its applications are dispersed and varied throughout the world, its foundation converges within one's own person. One who practices ritual simply seeks it within himself and pays heed to his words and conduct. For words are the outward manifestation of conduct: if conduct does not match one's words, it is not cultivated. Conduct is the substance of words: if words do not match one's conduct, they do not accord with the Way. Truly, when the person is not cultivated, ritual cannot be practiced. Therefore, the gentleman puts self-governance first in his learning, and whatever he deliberates and speaks of, he follows in practice without overstepping; he exerts himself in careful cultivation, and whatever his spoken words set forth, he faithfully pursues…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:

無不矜也有居業之言則必立誠以居其業而
行無不謹也可謂善行矣夫行而曰善則行之
脩而言合於道也固禮之所由行哉吾知中倫
中慮比類以成其行此無體之精也而動作威
儀之則將由以出焉禮之防範人情盡品節之
詳者不根抵于是乎有物有恒著誠以去其偽
此無文之敬也而軌物度數之陳將由以舉焉
禮之紀綱人道極經綸之大者不統體于是乎
===
謂之曰禮之質也信乎君子之紀羣動者莫急
於禮而言而履之則莫切於身矣不然薄於德
於禮虛也吾如禮何哉夫禮何以本諸誠也蓋

之心入斯去禮遠矣故孔子告顏淵為仁曰克

punctuated:
而不違。有進德之言，則必忠信以進其德，而行無不矜也；有居業之言，則必立誠以居其業，而行無不謹也，可謂善行矣。夫行而曰善，則行之脩而言合於道也，固禮之所由行哉！吾知中倫中慮，比類以成其行，此無體之精也，而動作威儀之則將由以出焉。禮之防範人情、盡品節之詳者，不根抵于是乎？有物有恒，著誠以去其偽，此無文之敬也，而軌物度數之陳將由以舉焉。禮之紀綱人道、極經綸之大者，不統體于是乎？謂之曰「禮之質也」，信乎！君子之紀羣動者莫急於禮，而言而履之，則莫切於身矣。不然，薄於德，於禮虛也，吾如禮何哉！夫禮何以本諸誠也？蓋禮有竭情、有美文，于心之外內得之，暴慢邪僻之心入，斯去禮遠矣。故孔子告顏淵為仁曰「克己復禮」。夫克己之功，豈有先於言動乎？己克則禮復矣。孔子之所謂禮，固禮之質哉！學禮者慎無居其華也。

大人舉禮樂則天地將為昭焉
translation_en:
…without violation. When there are words about advancing in virtue, one must use loyalty and trustworthiness to advance that virtue, so that in one's conduct there is nothing not held to a strict standard; when there are words about abiding in one's work, one must establish sincerity to abide in that work, so that in one's conduct there is nothing not cautious—this may be called good conduct! Now when conduct is called good, it means that conduct is cultivated and words accord with the Way; is this not indeed whereby ritual is put into practice! I know that hitting the mark of human relationships and hitting the mark of deliberation, matching categories to complete one's conduct—this is the essence of ritual that has no fixed body, and the rules of movement and dignified demeanor will emerge from it. Does not ritual's regulation of human feelings and exhaustion of the details of grades and distinctions have its root here? Having substance and having constancy, manifesting sincerity to cast out falsehood—this is the reverence that has no outward ornament, and the array of standards and numerical degrees will be raised up through it. Does not ritual's ordering of the human Way and reaching the utmost greatness of statecraft find its unifying body here? To call it "the substance of ritual" is truly fitting! In the gentleman's ordering of the myriad activities, nothing is more urgent than ritual, and in speaking and treading it out in practice, nothing is more closely tied to one's own person. Otherwise, if one is thin in virtue, one's ritual is hollow—what can I do with ritual then! Now why is ritual rooted in sincerity? Because ritual has the exhaustion of genuine feeling and has refined pattern, obtained from outside and inside the mind; once a violent, negligent, perverse, or depraved mind enters, one is far removed from ritual. Therefore Confucius, in telling Yan Yuan (顏淵) how to practice benevolence, said, "Overcome the self and return to ritual." Now in the work of overcoming the self, how could there be anything prior to words and actions? When the self is overcome, ritual is restored. What Confucius called ritual is indeed the substance of ritual! Those who study ritual must be careful not to dwell merely in its flowery ornament.

"When the great man holds up ritual and music, Heaven and Earth will be made bright thereby."

Associate Examiner Acting Director Wu comments: "Grasps the meaning of how institutional creation assists transformation; one who is profound in the Classic of Rites."
Associate Examiner Examining Editor Zhao comments: "An essay that expounds principle, concise, substantial, and worthy of emulation."

The sage's creation of rites and music is the means by which he assists and manifests transformation and nurture. Now, what the sage values is assisting transformation; therefore, when he institutes rites and music, Heaven and Earth are made radiant thereby. Is this not the mechanism of sympathetic resonance between things of the same kind? The recorder of the text in effect says: The Way of rites and music has its foundation in emulating the patterns of nature, and thus it also has the function of bringing capacities to completion; in sum, it simply awaits the right person before it can be put into practice. I find verification of this in the deeds of the Great Man. Possessing the virtue of a sage and occupying the position of the Son of Heaven, he concentrates his spirit and embodies the Way, having already encompassed within his mind the essence of creating institutions; when governance is settled and achievements are brought to completion, he further in his own person meets the opportune moment for creating institutions. Abiding in what he preserves, rites are instituted in accordance with Earth: grounded in the order of utmost sequence, their warp and woof are established, and ritual distinctions and refinements are made complete herein. Savouring what he delights in, music is created from Heaven: grounded in the flow of utmost harmony, its sounds and vital breaths issue forth, and human nature and feelings are expressed herein. When the Great Man institutes rites and music in this manner, we shall see that once the mysteries of creation are revealed in his institutional creations, the achievement of assisting transformation naturally reaches above and below. Qian knows the Great Beginning, rousing the emergence of transformation and nurture, yet without harmony it cannot proceed; once the Great Man institutes music, he summons harmony with harmony, and the Way of Heaven will thereby be made radiant! 物，鼓化育之入也，而不得序則不立；大人一興禮，則以序召序，地道將焉昭矣。闡之爲明備之休，而天地可官焉，一施一受，若其所推行也；建之爲中和之極，而天地可位焉，或運或處，若其所隆施也。是神化之能事，備于禮樂；而制作之全功，極于參贊矣。此非大人窮天地之神也，何以臻此哉？雖然，有本焉。古之聖王，日閑其心于和順，而邪僻無由以入，是以性情之德不蕩，而造化之應無違焉。故路鼗、土鼓，可協神人；杯飲、汚尊，可脩祀享。彼所以孚之者，豈在聲容度數間哉？語曰：「禮樂不可妄興也。」故必有聖人之德而後可。

translation_en:
… things, rousing the incoming movement of transformative nurture, yet without order it cannot be established; once the great man institutes ritual, order summons forth order, and how shall the Way of Earth not be made manifest therein? Expounding them into the glorious perfection of clarity and completeness, Heaven and Earth can thereby be governed in their proper offices—one bestowing, one receiving, as if pushed forward by his practice; establishing them as the ultimate standard of equilibrium and harmony, Heaven and Earth can thereby be set in their proper places—one revolving, one abiding, as if generously conferred by him. Thus the consummate work of mysterious transformation is complete in ritual and music, and the total achievement of creating institutions reaches its peak in assisting and participating in the cosmic order. Were it not that the great man exhausts the spirit of Heaven and Earth, how could he attain to this? Even so, there is a root to it. The sage-kings of antiquity daily schooled their minds in harmony and compliance so that perversity and depravity had no way to enter; therefore the virtue of their nature and feelings did not go astray, and the response of the creative transformations did not go against them. Hence with road-hand-drums and earthen drums, they could bring spirits and men into harmony; drinking from cupped hands and scooping wine from hollowed-out ground, they could properly conduct sacrificial offerings. How could that whereby they inspired sincere trust lie merely among sounds, appearances, measures, and numbers? As the saying goes: "Ritual and music must not be rashly instituted." Therefore, only when one possesses the virtue of a sage is it possible.

The empire cannot be governed by clinging to a single method of governance. One must examine what is appropriate to the times and understand the essentials of governance, and only then can one adapt to changes inexhaustibly. Now, as for what are called the essentials of governance: the application of leniency or strictness, relaxation or urgency, and the institution of complexity or simplicity, substance or refinement—each has what it values, which cannot be altered. title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
乍寬乍嚴朝文而莫質譬之猶浮江河亡維楫
也鮮克濟矣然不惟其時之宜而泥於已然一
定之迹以為之體顧乃執寬以議嚴執文以訾
質則亦固焉而不通而於治道均病矣譬之猶
膠柱而鼓瑟也其何調之有夫惟聖人能與世
推移追俗變化審其時之所宜用者而尚之以
為治治體既定然後守其術以要其成不搖於
眾人之說不易於一時之利夫是以政成而人
安之易曰通其變使民不倦神而化之使民宜
===
之此識體之論也且夫天下之事莫不有體焉
紆朱懷金肅拜而端議朝廷之體也而以之施
於山林則駭矣長佩緩帶矩步而雅歌膠序之
體也而以之應於軍旅則迂矣然則治天下之
體而可以一端盡邪是故捄僿者以質而捄野
者以文非惡夫質而故文之也所捄之體異也
處疆者利用惠而處弱者利用威非惡夫惠而
故威之也所處之體異也蓋嘗考之古矣夏道
俊威殷人先罰同民而異化周公愼始君陳和

作寬作嚴朝文而莫質譬之猶浮江河亡維檝
也鮮克濟矣然不惟其時之宜而泥於已然一
定之迹以爲之體顧乃執寬以議嚴執文以訾

衆人之說不易於一時之利夫是以政成而人
安之易曰通其變使民不倦神而化之使民宜
===
之此識體之論也且夫天下之事莫不有體焉
紆朱懷金肅拜而端議朝廷之體也而以之施
於山林則駭矣長佩緩帶矩步而雅歌膠序之
體也而以之施於軍旅則迂矣然則治天下之
體而可以一端盡耶是故棣儀者以質而棣野
者以文非惡夫質而故文之也所棣之體異也
處彊者利用惠而處弱者利用威非惡夫惠而
故威之也所處之體異也蓋嘗考之古矣夏道
做威殷人先罰同民而異化周公愼始君陳和
punctuated:
乍寬乍嚴，朝文而莫質，譬之猶浮江河亡維楫也，鮮克濟矣。然不惟其時之宜，而泥於已然一定之迹以為之體，顧乃執寬以議嚴，執文以訾質，則亦固焉而不通，而於治道均病矣。譬之猶膠柱而鼓瑟也，其何調之有？夫惟聖人能與世推移，追俗變化，審其時之所宜用者而尚之以為治。治體既定，然後守其術以要其成，不搖於眾人之說，不易於一時之利，夫是以政成而人安之。《易》曰：「通其變，使民不倦；神而化之，使民宜之。」此識體之論也。
且夫天下之事，莫不有體焉。紆朱懷金，肅拜而端議，朝廷之體也，而以之施於山林則駭矣；長佩緩帶，矩步而雅歌，膠序之體也，而以之應於軍旅則迂矣。然則治天下之體，而可以一端盡邪？是故捄僿者以質，而捄野者以文，非惡夫質而故文之也，所捄之體異也；處疆者利用惠，而處弱者利用威，非惡夫惠而故威之也，所處之體異也。蓋嘗考之古矣：夏道俊威，殷人先罰，同民而異化；周公愼始，君陳和
translation_en:
…now lenient and now strict, refined in the morning and unadorned by evening—this is like floating on the Yangtze or the Yellow River without a mooring rope or an oar; rarely can one succeed in crossing. Yet if one does not consider what is appropriate to the times, and instead clings to the fixed traces of the past as one's governing framework—clinging to leniency to criticize strictness, or clinging to refinement to disparage unadorned simplicity—then one becomes obstinate and inflexible, which is equally harmful to the way of governance. This is like gluing down the bridges to play a zither; what harmony could there possibly be? Only the sage is able to shift along with the age and transform in response to customs, examining what is suitable to employ in his time and exalting it so as to bring about order. Once the governing framework is established, he then holds fast to its methods to see it through to completion, unswayed by the arguments of the multitude and unaltered by momentary advantage; therefore, governance is accomplished and the people find peace in it. The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "By carrying through its changes, they kept the people from growing weary; by spirit-like transformation, they made the people find it fitting." This is a discourse on understanding the fundamental framework.

Moreover, among all affairs under heaven, there is none that does not have its proper form. Trailing vermilion cords and carrying gold seals, bowing in solemn reverence and deliberating uprightly—this is the proper form of the royal court; yet if one were to apply it to the mountains and forests, it would cause alarm. Wearing long pendants and loose sashes, walking with measured steps and singing elegant odes—this is the proper form of the schools and academies; yet if one were to use it to respond to military campaigns, it would be impractically pedantic. How, then, could the framework for governing the empire be exhausted by a single approach? Therefore, one remedies superficiality with unadorned simplicity, and remedies rusticity with cultural refinement; it is not that one despises simplicity and deliberately makes things refined, but that the condition being remedied is different. One situated in strength finds it advantageous to employ kindness, while one situated in weakness finds it advantageous to employ awe-inspiring authority; it is not that one despises kindness and deliberately exercises authority, but that the situation in which one stands is different. Indeed, I have examined this in antiquity: the way of the Xia magnified awe-inspiring dignity [?], while the people of Yin put punishment first—the people were the same, yet the transformative teachings differed; the Duke of Zhou (Zhou Gong) was cautious at the beginning, while Jun Chen harmonized…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
□而異政夫禹與周公皆聖人也而成湯
□□承之顧悉矯其治而不嫌而仲尼之論政
也則欲正名於衛諭臣於魯節禮於齊悅邇來
遠於楚亦往往異焉抑豈皆有意於爲異哉道
以世移政由俗革卽聖人莫能違之矣代而下
也知是道者吾獨有取於漢之文宣焉漢興承
亡秦之敝民厭苛法文帝知其體之在於息民
也於是沛然順流與之休息鎭之以玄默守之
以恭儉寧疏法制缺禮樂而不敢以稽古改制
之事先於劭農蠲租之令迨武昭以來上下相
蒙官職寢廢宣帝知其體之在於更化也於是
密樞機覈名實賞信誅必以彊主威寧守漢道
謝周制而終不敢爲因循委靡之政以隳吾英
明果斷之功卒之文有俗易刑錯之隆而宣亦
有吏稱民安之效盛業光美竝爲漢宗誠各得
其要也藉令當孝文之世而曰曷不爲綜核之
明作當孝宣之時而曰曷不爲清靜之寡事是
猶責扶羸者曰曷不爲鍼砭之利責攻疾者曰

punctuated: □而異政。夫禹與周公皆聖人也，而成湯、□□承之，顧悉矯其治而不嫌。而仲尼之論政也，則欲正名於衛、諭臣於魯、節禮於齊、悅邇來遠於楚，亦往往異焉。抑豈皆有意於爲異哉？道以世移，政由俗革，卽聖人莫能違之矣。代而下也，知是道者，吾獨有取於漢之文、宣焉。漢興，承亡秦之敝，民厭苛法。文帝知其體之在於息民也，於是沛然順流，與之休息，鎭之以玄默，守之以恭儉，寧疏法制、缺禮樂，而不敢以稽古改制之事，先於劭農蠲租之令。迨武、昭以來，上下相蒙，官職寢廢。宣帝知其體之在於更化也，於是密樞機、覈名實，賞信誅必，以彊主威，寧守漢道、謝周制，而終不敢爲因循委靡之政，以隳吾英明果斷之功。卒之，文有俗易刑錯之隆，而宣亦有吏稱民安之效，盛業光美，竝爲漢宗，誠各得其要也。藉令當孝文之世，而曰「曷不爲綜核之明作？」當孝宣之時，而曰「曷不爲清靜之寡事？」是猶責扶羸者曰「曷不爲鍼砭之利？」責攻疾者曰
translation_en: …[middle?] and yet their governance differed. Now Yu 禹 and the Duke of Zhou 周公 were both sages, and yet when Cheng Tang 成湯 and [Jun Chen 君陳?] succeeded them, they completely rectified their predecessors' governance without hesitation. And when Zhongni 仲尼 [Confucius] discussed governance, he wished to rectify names in Wei 衛, instruct the ministers in Lu 魯, regulate rites in Qi 齊, and please those near so as to attract those far away in Chu 楚—thus also frequently varying his approach. Yet how could they all have intentionally sought to be different? The Way shifts with the age, and governance changes according to customs; even a sage cannot go against this. Coming down through later generations, among those who understood this Way, I take especial note of Emperors Wen 文 and Xuan 宣 of the Han 漢. When the Han arose, it inherited the exhaustion left by the fallen Qin 秦, and the people were weary of harsh laws. Emperor Wen knew that the proper form of governance lay in giving rest to the people. Thereupon, going smoothly with the current, he granted them rest and recuperation, calming them with quiet non-action and maintaining it with reverence and frugality. He preferred to leave legal statutes loose and rites and music incomplete, rather than dare to place the business of investigating antiquity and reforming institutions ahead of decrees encouraging agriculture and remitting taxes. By the time following Emperors Wu 武 and Zhao 昭, superiors and inferiors deceived one another, and official duties fell gradually into neglect. Emperor Xuan knew that the proper form of governance lay in reforming instruction. Thereupon, he tightened the pivot of state affairs and verified that realities matched names, making rewards trustworthy and punishments certain so as to strengthen the ruler's authority. He preferred to hold to the Han way and decline the institutions of Zhou, and to the end dared not engage in routine and spiritless governance lest he ruin his achievements of brilliant discernment and resolute decision. In the end, Emperor Wen achieved the flourishing state of transformed customs and punishments set aside unused, while Emperor Xuan likewise achieved the effect of officials being equal to their duties and the people being at peace. Their grand enterprises were glorious and admirable, and both became honored ancestors of the Han; truly, each grasped what was essential for his time. Suppose that in the age of the Filial Wen someone had said, "Why not engage in the brisk exertion of comprehensive verification?" or in the time of the Filial Xuan someone had said, "Why not practice the sparse affairs of pure tranquility?" This would be like reproaching one who is nursing an emaciated patient by saying, "Why not use the sharpness of acupuncture needles and stone probes?" or reproaching one who is attacking an acute illness by saying,…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
曷不為呴噓之適也豈不繆哉是故治身者攻
養殊術歸於葆生治世者寬嚴殊政期於致平
善乎崔子之言之也為國之法有似理身平則
致養疾則攻焉通斯說者可以語治體矣或曰
仁義竝用人主之術今必審其時之所宜者而
專尚之以為治其無乃溺於偏而傷於化歟吁
不然盍亦觀諸天乎陽居大夏陰居大冬而燠
寒異焉夫冬豈無一日之燠而夏豈無一日之
寒要以不失其陰陽之體而已然則治道之所
===
謂尚寬者夫豈弛然而無斷其所謂尚嚴者夫
豈慘然而少恩要亦不失其寬嚴之體而已由
斯言之即治有所尚亦何害於人主之術哉雖
然此特權時捄敝之論耳箕子之陳三德也曰
平康正直自平康之世遠而後剛克柔克之權
始有所偏用於天下非聖人意也勢也昔者周
之初造殷民未靖不得已嚴制而曲防之歷成
而康拊摩涵育且數十年而梗化之俗易於是
畢公尹東郊康王命之曰不剛不柔厥德允脩

punctuated: 「曷不為呴噓之適也？」豈不繆哉！是故治身者，攻養殊術，歸於葆生；治世者，寬嚴殊政，期於致平。善乎崔子之言之也：「為國之法，有似理身，平則致養，疾則攻焉。」通斯說者，可以語治體矣。或曰：「仁義竝用，人主之術。今必審其時之所宜者而專尚之以為治，其無乃溺於偏而傷於化歟？」吁，不然！盍亦觀諸天乎？陽居大夏，陰居大冬，而燠寒異焉。夫冬豈無一日之燠，而夏豈無一日之寒？要以不失其陰陽之體而已。然則治道之所謂尚寬者，夫豈弛然而無斷？其所謂尚嚴者，夫豈慘然而少恩？要亦不失其寬嚴之體而已。由斯言之，即治有所尚，亦何害於人主之術哉！雖然，此特權時捄敝之論耳。箕子之陳三德也，曰：「平康正直。」自平康之世遠，而後剛克、柔克之權始有所偏用於天下，非聖人意也，勢也。昔者周之初造，殷民未靖，不得已嚴制而曲防之。歷成而康，拊摩涵育且數十年，而梗化之俗易。於是畢公尹東郊，康王命之曰：「不剛不柔，厥德允脩。」…
translation_en:
… “Why do you not provide the comfort of gentle breathing and warming?” Would that not be absurd! Therefore, for those who regulate the body, attacking illness and nourishing vitality are different methods, yet both aim at preserving life; for those who govern the world, leniency and severity are different policies, yet both aim at achieving peace. Well indeed did Master Cui (Cui Shi 崔寔) state it: “The method of governing a state is like regulating the body: when healthy, one devotes oneself to nourishment; when ill, one attacks the ailment.” One who comprehends this theory can speak of the fundamental principles of governance.

Someone might ask: “Employing benevolence and righteousness together is the art of the ruler. Now, if one must examine what is appropriate for the time and exclusively prioritize it in governing, will that not sink into partiality and harm moral transformation?” Ah, not so! Why not observe Heaven? Yang resides in high summer and yin resides in deep winter, so warmth and cold differ accordingly. Yet how could winter lack a single day of warmth, or summer lack a single day of cold? The essential point is simply that they do not lose the fundamental character of yin and yang. This being the case, in the Way of governance, how could what is called prioritizing leniency mean being lax and indecisive? And how could what is called prioritizing severity mean being harsh and devoid of grace? The essential point is likewise simply not losing the fundamental character of leniency or severity. Spoken of in this light, even if governance has that which it prioritizes, what harm is that to the art of the ruler!

Even so, this is merely a discourse on weighing the times to remedy defects. When Viscount Ji (Jizi 箕子) set forth the Three Virtues, he said: “In peace and tranquility, uprightness and correctness.” Only after the age of peace and tranquility receded did the expedient measures of prevailing by firmness and prevailing by gentleness begin to be applied with partial emphasis in the world; this was not the intention of the sages, but the force of circumstances. In antiquity, at the founding of the Zhou, the people of Yin were not yet pacified, so out of necessity the rulers strictly controlled them and guarded against them in every detail. Passing through the reigns of King Cheng and King Kang, they comforted, nurtured, and cultivated them for several decades until the customs that obstructed transformation were changed. Thereupon, when the Duke of Bi (Bi Gong 畢公) governed the eastern outskirts, King Kang charged him, saying: “Neither terlalu firm nor too gentle, his virtue is truly cultivated.” …

text:

是為仁義道德之師魯國多賢非無才辯
聰明之士然千古不傳之祕惟二人獨得
其眞回也深潛專心克己參乎誠確篤志
省身仁能三月之不違勇則萬人而必往

出于金石其在及門之彥並為入室之英

punctuated: 文德之純。拭目竦瞻，盟心誦法。竊以尼丘誕聖，是為仁義道德之師；魯國多賢，非無才辯聰明之士。然千古不傳之祕，惟二人獨得其眞。回也深潛，專心克己；參乎誠確，篤志省身。仁能三月之不違，勇則萬人而必往。陋巷是處，樂無改于簞瓢；敝裘而耕，歌若出于金石。其在及門之彥，並為入室之英。耿光既炙乎秋陽，速化遂霑乎時雨。立如卓爾，知見道之益親；一以貫之，幸聞言而卽唯。蓋默識心通之妙，繇眞積力久而成。雖具體猶微，未入聖人之域；然聞風皆起，允為儒者之宗。往哲既遐，微言幾墜。卽章縫末學，罕能涉其津涯；矧旒纊至尊，何暇尋其軌轍？唐室之褒封甚侈，徒飾彌文；宋祖之賛述雖工，詎探奧義？豈如上聖，克紹眞儒。恭惟皇帝陛下，體睿含靈，
translation_en:
… the purity of your civil virtue. Wiping our eyes, we gaze up in awe, and pledge in our hearts to recite and emulate it.

We humbly reflect that Mount Ni gave birth to the Sage [Confucius], who became the teacher of benevolence, righteousness, the Way, and its virtue; and although the state of Lu had many worthies, it was not lacking in men of talent, eloquence, and intelligence. Yet of the secrets unhurriedly passed down and untaught for a thousand ages, only two men alone grasped the true essence. Hui [Yan Hui 顏回] was deeply immersed, focusing his mind on overcoming the self; Shen [Zeng Shen 曾參] was sincere and steadfast, dedicating his will to daily self-examination. The one’s benevolence did not lapse for three months; the other’s courage was such that he would go forward even against ten thousand men. Dwelling in a mean alley, Yan Hui’s joy was unaltered by a single bamboo dish of rice and a gourd of drink; plowing in a worn fur coat, Zeng Shen’s singing rang out as if from metal and stone. Among the accomplished scholars who came to the Master's gate, both were the finest who entered his inner chamber. Warmed by his bright glory like the autumn sun, their rapid transformation was moistened as by timely rain. Seeing something "standing lofty before him," Yan Hui knew his perception of the Way had grown ever closer; hearing that "one thread runs through it all," Zeng Shen was fortunate to hear the words and immediately answer "Yes!" Indeed, the subtlety of their silent comprehension and mental mastery was achieved through genuine accumulation and prolonged effort. Although they possessed the sage's qualities in miniature and had not yet entered the realm of the Sage himself, all who heard of their character were inspired to rise up, and they truly became the patriarchs of Confucian scholars.

Once the former wise men had passed into the distance, their subtle words were nearly lost. Even minor scholars in ceremonial caps and robes could rarelyford the shores of their learning; how much less could the supreme sovereign, wearing the imperial crown with pendant jade, find the leisure to trace their footsteps? The Tang house's enfeoffments and praises were lavish indeed, yet merely adorned superficial ritual; the Song founder's eulogies were skillful, yet how could they fathom the profound meaning? How could they compare to the Supreme Sage, who is able to carry on the legacy of the true Confucians?

We reverently consider Your Majesty the Emperor, embodying sagely wisdom and encompassing spiritual intelligence, …
