punctuated: 窮神知化，守恭默而思道，秉敬一以宅心。陟降紹庭，邁日就月將之益；中和建極，會金聲玉振之全。方仰追堯、舜之隆，乃俯切顏、曾之慕。謂明王盛帝，務學何取于英華；彼亞聖大賢，悟道皆由于篤實。撮其體要，著爲箴言。玄之又玄，契齋心坐忘之旨；妄復無妄，明誠意謹獨之方。渾噩之詞不煩，易簡而理自得。若虞廷相授，宛然十六字之文；猶《魯頌》無邪，能蓋三百篇之義。寫之琬琰，詢于芻蕘。宸藻奎章，寵賁絲綸之地；神謨聖訓，儼垂戶牖之銘。共傳丹扆之芳規，式侈黃扉之盛事。臣等性終愚魯，職在贊襄。未若臯陶之載賡，徒有南容之三復。敢不書紳觸目，用比韋弦；尚絅立心，無慚屋漏。承勿僞之
translation_en:
… fathoming the numinous and knowing transformation, maintaining reverent silence while contemplating the Way, and holding fast to reverence and unity to settle the mind. Ascending and descending to continue the legacy of the ancestral court, You surpass the daily progress and monthly advances of learning; establishing the supreme standard through equilibrium and harmony, You gather the complete symphony of bronze bells and jade chimes. Just as You look up to pursue the grandeur of Yao 堯 and Shun 舜, so too do You bow down in earnest admiration of Yan Hui 顏回 and Zengzi 曾子. You hold that when enlightened kings and flourishing emperors devote themselves to learning, what need have they for mere flowery ornament? And that when those Second Sages and great worthies awakened to the Way, it was always through earnest solidity. Extracting their essential substance, You composed them into admonitions. Mystery upon mystery, they tally with the purport of fasting the mind and sitting in forgetfulness; returning from falsehood to freedom from falsehood, they illuminate the method of making the intentions sincere and being watchful over oneself when alone. The unadorned and solemn words are free of verbosity—easy and simple, yet the principle is naturally grasped. They are like the mutual transmission at the court of Yu 虞, vividly recalling the sixteen-character text; or like the phrase "having no depraved thoughts" in the Odes of Lu (Lu song 魯頌), capable of encompassing the meaning of all three hundred poems of the Classic of Poetry. Inscribing them upon fine jade, You yet consult the humble grass- and firewood-gatherers. Imperial compositions of stellar brilliance graciously adorn the place where silken decrees are drafted; divine counsels and sagely instructions hang solemnly like inscriptions upon doors and windows. All pass on the fragrant rules from behind the vermilion screen, magnifying this splendid occasion within the yellow doors of the Grand Secretariat.

Your servants are by nature irredeemably dull and obtuse, yet our office lies in assisting and advising. Unable to match Gao Yao 臯陶 in continuing the song, we can only emulate Nan Rong 南容 in repeating the lines thrice. How could we dare not write them upon our sashes to keep them before our eyes, using them like soft leather and taut bowstrings to correct our faults; or wear plain cloth over embroidered robes in establishing our minds, so as to feel no shame even in the secluded northwest corner of the house? Receiving the … of "no falsehood," …

translation_en:
Associate Examiner and Examining Editor Wang 王 comments: Worrying in times of good order and sensing danger in times of enlightened rule—who does not know this, and who cannot speak of it? Yet there has never been an essay as incisive, loyal, and forthright as this one. It should be recorded as an aid to preserving peace and prosperity.

Associate Examiner and Junior Compiler Gong 公 comments: Its sincere loyalty and affection, and its forthright and upright arguments, are vividly apparent as one reads it. It should be recorded for presentation to the throne.

Associate Examiner and Junior Compiler Liu 劉 comments: To remain vigilant when there is no cause for anxiety—such is how a minister and subject ought to render loyalty. Moreover, it traces the root back to His Majesty's pure heart-and-mind in order to rectify the source of transformation and thereby prolong peace and blessings; it may truly serve as fine counsel for the imperial throne.

Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Zhu 朱 comments: Our Emperor exerts his spirit in seeking good governance and daily wishes to hear words of mutual admonition so as to rival the splendor of Yu 虞 and Zhou 周. You are able to discourse on this continuously and coherently, hitting upon all the essential points and truly displaying loyal sincerity; it may be presented to the throne.

Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting Shen 申 comments: It brings forth the import of vigilance and admonition, analyzing it point by point without omission, while maintaining an impassioned argument and the utmost earnestness in loyalty and affection. …pointing to personally grasping decision-making and broadening the reception of advice as the essentials for Our August Emperor in preserving great peace and prosperity—is he not indeed a scholar who cherishes loyal sincerity and harbors far-reaching plans? I respectfully record it for presentation.

Is the cycle of order and disorder, stability and peril, brought about by the timing of Heaven? Or is the pivot for securing order and maintaining stability brought about by the mind of the ruler? Now, suppose that as Heaven shapes the times, an era of order were guaranteed never to fall into disorder, and an era of stability were guaranteed never to fall into peril; then a ruler could calmly possess the pleasures of order and stability forever, and what need would there be for anxiety? Or suppose that the alternation of order and disorder, stability and peril, arrived as inevitably as cold and heat or day and night; then one could simply consign fate to chance, and again there would be no need for anxiety. It is only because the movement of times in Heaven both builds upon and leans against itself in ways that cannot be foreknown, while its pivot always rests in the single mind of the ruler—if he controls it, there is order; if he neglects it, there is disorder; if he upholds it, there is stability; if he shakes it, there is peril; disaster can be dissolved before it takes form, yet calamity constantly springs from the tiniest subtleties—that the mind of an enlightened ruler cannot but be cautiously and anxiously vigilant. Therefore, he does not rely on order being constant, but relies on possessing the counsels for securing order; he does not rely on stability being constant, but relies on possessing the methods for maintaining stability. By means of this Way, the emperors and kings of antiquity prayed for an enduring Mandate and attained supreme governance, enjoyed great enterprises and left behind glorious names. Indeed, since the days of knotted cords and notched tallies, among all ages praised by the world as having reached the utmost order and highest stability, none have been more revered than Yu and Zhou. title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
虞四海聲教兩階干羽斯何時也而君
欽亮臣曰儆戒明良喜起交口一心方周
道之郅隆鸑鷟在岡斑斑在囿朱干玉戚
在廟四夷九譯在朝而君曰懲毖臣曰張
皇咨殷鑒夏不徐徐焉裔是而降賈傅當
園土幾虚之世焦然蒿目奮其二流涕六
太息之談而文帝亦嘔喻受之魏鄭公丁
外闔不掩之時愀然動容納其十漸十思
之誡而太宗毎竦意覽焉是知明哲之主
===
皆不狃盛治以忘憂忠藎之臣皆不諱危
言以竭慮何若是汲汲歟今夫有人於此
其精神容澤起居飲食素彊亡恙也乃因
而廢衛生養形之言越人倉公必挟鍼石
而議其後是何也則彊之不足恃也天下
之勢胡以異此愚嘗玄覽古今追跡興替
諸不暇具論論其章章較著者漢至建始
元壽之間席武宣之遺烈猶赫然臣單于
朝昆彌而房闥之葭莩乃拱手而移其祚

translation_en:
…the house of Yu [Shun], when royal prestige and teaching reached throughout the Four Seas and shields and feathers were danced between the two staircases—what an era that was! Yet the sovereign was reverentlyattentive to heaven's work [or: said "Be reverent and aid me"], and his ministers spoke of vigilance and caution; the enlightened ruler and his worthy ministers rejoiced and rose up together, exchanging counsel with a single mind. When the Way of Zhou was at its grandest height, phoenixes perched on the ridges, beasts of mottled coat roamed in the royal parks, vermilion shields and jade battle-axes were displayed in the ancestral temple, and the Four Barbarians came to court through ninefold interpretation—yet the sovereign spoke of learning from past reverses to guard against future ills, and the ministers spoke of magnifying the royal sway, consulting the lessons of Yin and taking warning from Xia without a moment's slackening.

Coming down from those eras: Tutor Jia [Jia Yi 賈誼], in an age when the prisons were nearly empty, looked on the world with anxious, furrowed brow and boldly set forth his discourse of "two things to weep over and six to sigh deeply at," and Emperor Wen [of Han] received it with gentle, appreciative warmth. Duke Zheng of Wei [Wei Zheng 魏徵], at a time when outer gates did not need to be shut at night, with solemn countenance presented his admonitions on the "ten gradual lapses" and "ten things to reflect upon," and Emperor Taizong [of Tang] invariably perused them with respectful attention. From this we know that enlightened and wise rulers never grow so accustomed to flourishing governance as to forget anxiety, and loyal, devoted ministers never shy away from alarming words in exhausting their forethought. Why were they so urgently restless?

Suppose there is a man here whose vitality, complexion, daily movements, and appetite have always been robust and free of illness; if on that account he rejects all advice on preserving life and nourishing the body, then Bian Que [Yueren 越人] and Chunyuyi [Canggong 倉公] will surely grasp their acupuncture needles and stone probes and predict his aftermath. Why is this? Because robustness alone cannot be relied upon. How is the condition of the empire any different from this?

I have privately surveyed antiquity and the present, tracing the footsteps of rise and fall. Leaving aside what there is no leisure to discuss in full, let us speak of the most clear and conspicuous examples. When the Han reached the Jianshi (32–29 BCE) and Yuanshou (2–1 BCE) reigns, resting upon the inherited glory of Emperors Wu and Xuan, it still awesomely made a vassal of the Chanyu [of the Xiongnu] and received the Kunmi [of Wusun] at court—yet slender-reed in-laws from the inner chambers were able, with folded hands, to usurp its throne;…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
唐之天寶編戶百萬非不號泰平也而羯
羠之么豎得鋌起而危其國夫釁有啓於
無虞而患每生於所忽此無他故焉大都
狃於積安之形疎於却慮之畫而不虞其
天之不足恃以至此也嗚呼斯詎非千世
之明戒哉是故身彊而彌攝者延歷之至
術也時寧而彌憂者保祚之長策也明主
知其然是以先霜戒冰未雨徹土天下方
波恬塵清櫜弓臥鼓而其心恒若有旦莫
===
===
杌隉之形天下方歲成蜡通室盈廩腐而
其心恒若有暑寒怨咨之聲天下方川岳
貢禎郊藪遊靈而其心恒若有恠異謫告
之符卒之家國無瑕命祚滋遠若見夫明
主之日廻用其憂而不知其有憂者乃其所
以無憂也易不云乎危者安其位者也亡
者保其存者也亂者有其治者也城復之
危日中之警聖人於泰豐屢致意焉蓋其
指深矣哉

punctuated: 唐之天寶，編戶百萬，非不號泰平也，而羯羠之么豎，得鋌起而危其國。夫釁有啓於無虞，而患每生於所忽。此無他故焉，大都狃於積安之形，疎於却慮之畫，而不虞其天之不足恃，以至此也。嗚呼！斯詎非千世之明戒哉？是故身彊而彌攝者，延歷之至術也；時寧而彌憂者，保祚之長策也。明主知其然，是以先霜戒冰，未雨徹土。天下方波恬塵清，櫜弓臥鼓，而其心恒若有旦莫杌隉之形；天下方歲成蜡通，室盈廩腐，而其心恒若有暑寒怨咨之聲；天下方川岳貢禎，郊藪遊靈，而其心恒若有恠異謫告之符。卒之家國無瑕，命祚滋遠。若見夫明主之日廻用其憂，而不知其有憂者，乃其所以無憂也。《易》不云乎：「危者，安其位者也；亡者，保其存者也；亂者，有其治者也。」城復之危，日中之警，聖人於《泰》、《豐》屢致意焉，蓋其指深矣哉！
translation_en: In the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, with millions of registered households, it was not that the empire could not be called peaceful; yet a petty wretch of Jie and Di stock was able to rise up in reckless rebellion and endanger the state. Indeed, crises are sometimes triggered when there is no cause for alarm, and disasters regularly arise from what is neglected. There is no other reason for this: in general, rulers grow accustomed to the appearance of accumulated peace, become lax in planning with far-sighted caution, and fail to anticipate that Heaven's favor cannot be relied upon, thereby coming to such a pass. Alas! Is this not a clear warning for a thousand generations? Therefore, taking ever greater care of oneself while the body is strong is the supreme art of prolonging life; being ever more anxious while the times are peaceful is the enduring policy for preserving the throne. The enlightened ruler knows this is so; thus, before the frost falls he guards against the coming ice, and before it rains he strips the mulberry roots to mend his house. Just when the realm has calm waves and settled dust, with bows cased and war-drums laid down, in his heart it is constantly as though there were signs of imminent peril and instability; just when the realm enjoys completed harvests and smoothly conducted year-end thanksgiving sacrifices, with households full and granaries overflowing to the point of rotting, in his heart it is constantly as though there were sounds of resentment and sighing over summer heat and winter cold; just when the realm sees rivers and mountains presenting auspicious omens and sacred creatures roaming the suburban marshes, in his heart it is constantly as though there were portents of strange anomalies and heavenly reproofs. In the end, the ruling house and the state remain without blemish, and the dynastic mandate grows ever more enduring. One may seem to see the enlightened ruler daily revolving [?] and exercising his anxiety, without realizing that his having anxiety is precisely the means by which he comes to be free of anxiety. Does the Book of Changes (Yi) not say: "He who falls into danger is he who feels secure in his position; he who perishes is he who takes his survival for granted; he who falls into disorder is he who presumes upon his good order"? With the danger of the city wall collapsing back into the moat, and the warning of the sun reaching midday, the sages repeatedly expressed their concern in the hexagrams Peace (Tai) and Abundance (Feng)—deep indeed was their meaning!

國家纂神明之統，履熾昌之運，幅員踰於萬里，文軌通於四夷。九列平衡以錯事，而權無旁落之憂；萬國輻輳以歸命，而勢無尾大之嫌。明天子又以聖哲照臨之，威德旁馳，中外具肅。五氣式序，九扈荐登；桴鼓之響稀聞，萑苻之區靡聚。邇歲强胡款塞，叛戎授首，諸幽遐辟絶之國、上代所不賓者，多奉琛執球，竭蹷以趨闕下。斯亦恬熈之盛際已！即謂之得天之時，軼漢、唐而接虞、周，夫誰曰不可？

然執事猶抱深恤，咨遠謨，欲爲國家設不必然之慮，儻亦儆戒張皇之意乎？敢不略效其愚。蓋聞泰寧既久，則瑕纇潛生；積習已成，則蠹壞從起。今之天下，以邊竟言之，若少寧矣；然武備未周，戎心叵測。間者增陴繕障，已詫固完；乃東胡一小入，
translation_en:
Our dynasty carries on the succession of divine brilliance and treads a course of flourishing prosperity; its territory exceeds ten thousand li, and uniform script and axle-widths extend to the four surrounding tribes. The Nine Ministers maintain an even balance in administering affairs, so there is no worry of power falling into outside hands; the myriad states converge like spokes at a hub in submitting to our mandate, so there is no suspicion of an overgrown tail in the balance of power. Moreover, the Enlightened Son of Heaven shines down upon it with sage wisdom; His awe-inspiring virtue speeds in all directions, and both the court and the provinces are wholly reverent. The five atmospheric influences follow their proper order, and the harvests overseen by the nine agricultural offices repeatedly come to fruition; the sound of alarm drums is rarely heard, and bandits in reed marshes no longer gather. In recent years, the powerful northern nomads have knocked at the frontier passes in submission, rebellious western tribes have offered up their heads, and those dark, distant, isolated, and remote lands that did not submit as guests in high antiquity now mostly present precious treasures and hold jade chimes, hastening with all their might to the gates of the palace. This is truly an era of tranquil and radiant splendour! Even if one were to say that we have attained the opportune time of Heaven, surpassing the Han and Tang and joining with Yu Shun and the Zhou, who would say it is not so?

Yet you, sir, still harbour deep solicitude and inquire after far-reaching counsels, wishing to make provision for contingencies on behalf of the dynasty that may not necessarily arise—is this not perhaps in the spirit of vigilance, caution, and strenuous preparation? How dare I not briefly offer my humble thoughts! For I have heard that when peace and tranquillity have lasted long, flaws and blemishes secretly grow; when ingrained habits have taken shape, decay and ruin arise therefrom. In the empire today, to speak of the frontiers, they seem somewhat at peace; yet military preparations are not thorough, and the intentions of the nomad tribes are unfathomable. Recently, having raised parapets and repaired frontier barriers, people have already boasted that our defences are solid and complete; yet when the eastern nomads made just a minor incursion, …

…immediately our troops were routed and our generals overthrown. Should the chieftains of the northern caitiffs break their covenant and lead their bow-drawing peoples to once again water their horses at the foot of the Great Wall, I am not convinced that our frontier officials are capable of managing what the military treatises call "relying on our own readiness to await them."

Speaking in terms of state finances, they seem somewhat relieved; yet frontier supplies and stipends for the princely establishments have accumulated years of arrears, the annual revenues of the Ministry of Revenue fall short of regular expenditures, the looms are exhausted below while the ministers who hold the counting rods tremble daily in fear of insufficiency above. Supposing unexpected floods like those of Yao's time or droughts like those of Tang's should suddenly arrive, wherewith would the state relieve them?

Official administration seems to be advancing steadily; yet names and realities have not been measured against one another, good and bad are confounded, and among the displaced commoners there are some who long for a happy land but cannot depart to it, or who gaze upon the "stone of redress" (jiashi) at court yet dare not state their grievances—this shows that officials are not yet entirely virtuous.

The customs of the literati seem to look upward in eager aspiration; yet the Great Way has long been eclipsed and decadent winds still blow. Scholars are urgent in their ambition to seek glory and compete for advancement while slighting quiet self-cultivation, and officeholders abound in schemes to cultivate connections and secure their emoluments while regarding independent integrity as impractical—this shows that the literati are not yet entirely encouraged to excellence.

Speaking from this perspective, to say that the present is neither well-governed nor peaceful is certainly impossible; yet to consequently declare that it has achieved enduring order and lasting peace, such that one may rest at ease without troubling the Sovereign's mind, is also an exaggeration. title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
響加遠居尊而倡者其應加疾人主欲諏
國家事而悉脩明之顧猶穆然負扆德意
不宣上下之間日以疏隔則人無悚厲之
心而事多苟且之弊卽有所注錯改張百
司且空文視之矣是故覽斷不可不親也
且夫豐蔀失晝煬竈蔽明人主寄一身于
天下之上事存奧渫則耳目不及接幾伏
眇忽則智慮不及周非延羣議擴四聰卽
世有禍萌難端將孰知而戒之是故聽納
===
不可不廣也今
聖主當春秋之寢盛乘
天步之正夷宜超然發
德音軫
睿慮
游神攬政儲思裁務時時
召見二三大臣討
累朝之故實省當世之闕遺於凡邊事
國計吏道世風諸如此類咸相與切磋究之

punctuated: 響加遠，居尊而倡者其應加疾。人主欲諏國家事而悉脩明之，顧猶穆然負扆，德意不宣，上下之間，日以疏隔，則人無悚厲之心，而事多苟且之弊，卽有所注錯改張，百司且空文視之矣。是故覽斷不可不親也。且夫豐蔀失晝，煬竈蔽明，人主寄一身于天下之上，事存奧渫，則耳目不及接；幾伏眇忽，則智慮不及周。非延羣議、擴四聰，卽世有禍萌難端，將孰知而戒之？是故聽納不可不廣也。今聖主當春秋之寢盛，乘天步之正夷，宜超然發德音，軫睿慮，游神攬政，儲思裁務，時時召見二三大臣，討累朝之故實，省當世之闕遺，於凡邊事、國計、吏道、世風，諸如此類，咸相與切磋究之，
translation_en: … echo reaches all the farther, and when one leads from an exalted position, the response comes all the swifter. When a ruler wishes to take counsel on affairs of state and thoroughly reform and clarify them, yet remains deeply withdrawn behind the throne-screen without making his virtuous intentions known, so that ruler and subjects grow more distant and estranged day by day, then men will lack hearts of reverent exertion and affairs will be rife with the abuses of perfunctoriness; even if measures are enacted or reforms undertaken, the hundred offices will treat them as mere empty words on paper. For this reason, personal perusal and decision-making cannot be neglected. Moreover, just as anluxuriant canopy blots out the daylight and standing before a blazing stove obscures one's vision, a ruler places his single person above the entire realm: when matters lie in hidden recesses, his eyes and ears cannot reach them; when subtle signs lurk in the minute and unseen, his wisdom and deliberation cannot encompass them all. Unless he invites the deliberations of the multitude and broadens his hearing in all four directions, even if the seeds of calamity and the beginnings of crisis exist in the world, who will know of them and guard against them? For this reason, listening to and accepting advice must be made broad. Now our Sacred Ruler is coming into the prime of his years and riding upon a time when Heaven's course is level and peaceful. He ought to transcendently issue his virtuous pronouncements, exercise his imperial concern, apply his spirit to grasping the reins of government, and store up thought to adjudicate affairs—frequently summoning two or three grand ministers to examine the precedents of successive reigns and inspect the omissions and shortcomings of the present age, so that with respect to all such matters as frontier affairs, state finances, the conduct of officials, and the customs of the age, they may mutually deliberate and thoroughly investigate them together, …

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
而又
垂矇誦之聽以啓讜議之門
采嫠恤之忠以恢直士之氣使天下悚焉知
上意之治不忘亂安不忘危如此也則庶幾羣
心濯磨百職競勸而天下之事可次第舉
矣雖然尤有要焉罔遊于逸罔淫于樂伯
益以之首規見可欲則思知足將興繕則
思知止玄成以之先誡蓋人主孰不利治
安而憚亂危者顧逸欲之感一入則儆惕
===
之慮頓移侈忭之意始形則豐豫之談爭
售而治亂安危之機于斯決矣故古之論
治者一本之君心易曰正其本萬事理此
之謂也
聖主誠能
覽昔賢之遺訓鏡理道之要原抑私嗜之微萌
遵愼終之令軌以幸羣生以規萬代將使
當時蒙治後世誦
聖皇皇乎無疆之大歷天其能違之哉

治者一本之君心易曰正其本萬事理此
之謂也
聖主誠能

遵慎終之令軌以章羣生以規萬代將使
當時蒙治後世誦
聖皇皇乎無疆之大歷天其能違之哉
punctuated: 而又垂矇誦之聽，以啓讜議之門；采嫠恤之忠，以恢直士之氣。使天下悚焉知上意之治不忘亂、安不忘危如此也，則庶幾羣心濯磨，百職競勸，而天下之事可次第舉矣。雖然，尤有要焉。「罔遊于逸，罔淫于樂」，伯益以之首規；「見可欲則思知足，將興繕則思知止」，玄成以之先誡。蓋人主孰不利治安而憚亂危者？顧逸欲之感一入，則儆惕之慮頓移；侈忭之意始形，則豐豫之談爭售，而治亂安危之機于斯決矣。故古之論治者，一本之君心。《易》曰：「正其本，萬事理。」此之謂也。聖主誠能覽昔賢之遺訓，鏡理道之要原，抑私嗜之微萌，遵愼終之令軌，以幸羣生，以規萬代，將使當時蒙治，後世誦聖，皇皇乎無疆之大歷，天其能違之哉！
translation_en:
…and furthermore, graciously lend an ear to the recitations of the blind musicians so as to open the gate to forthright counsel, and adopt the loyalty of the widow who worried for the state so as to invigorate the spirit of upright scholars. If the whole realm is thus moved with awe to know that His Majesty's intention is so mindful of disorder in times of order, and of peril in times of peace, then we may hope that all minds will be cleansed and polished, the hundred officials will vie with one another in diligence, and the affairs of the realm can be successfully undertaken in turn.

Even so, there is something still more fundamental. "Do not wander in idleness; do not indulge to excess in pleasure"—with these words Boyi 伯益 offered his foremost admonition. "When seeing what is desirable, think of knowing contentment; when about to undertake building and repairs, think of knowing where to stop"—with these words Xuancheng 玄成 [Wei Zheng 魏徵, Duke Wenzhen of Zheng] gave his primary warning. For what ruler does not find advantage in order and peace, and dread disorder and peril? Yet once the temptations of ease and desire enter, thoughts of vigilance and caution suddenly shift; once inclinations toward extravagance and delight begin to take shape, talk of abundance and comfort competes for favor—and at that point the pivot between order and disorder, peace and peril, is decided. Therefore, those in antiquity who discussed governance rooted it entirely in the mind of the ruler. When the Book of Changes (Yi 易) [as quoted in classical tradition] says, "Rectify the root, and the myriad affairs will be in order," this is what it means.

If our Sacred Ruler can truly peruse the bequeathed teachings of past worthies, use the essential source of the principles of governance as a mirror, curb the subtle stirrings of personal fondness, and follow the fine path of prudence to the very end, so as to bless all living beings and plan for ten thousand generations, it will cause the present age to enjoy good governance and posterity to praise his sagely virtue. Majestic indeed will be the boundless great destiny of the dynasty—how could Heaven possibly oppose it!

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
第二問
沈季文
同考試官署郎中吳批周禮本周公治定所制全書也顧
讀者亂之是作窮本原委曲斷以理足破千古之疑矣
同考試官檢討趙批考據精覈辨證詳切諸儒炫紛破析
之說此足為斷案矣
考試官侍讀學士申批學古通經斷之獨見必佳士也宜錄
考試官大學士張批博辨而有特識蓋經生之選也錄
===
聖經之不明於天下也談經者晦之也夫
聖人之心施於有政而布在方冊其所可
見者治之具也非其所以治也惟上智之
士焉能緣法以求心得心而忘象反是而
索諸儀章度數者下也索諸文字訓詁者
又其下也甚則臆決懸斷取聖人之經而
亂之昔人謂漢儒窮經之害慘於秦火非
有所激而云然哉乃今之亂經者又不止
漢儒巳也夫自漢惠除挾書之律孝武建

聖經之不明於天下也，談經者晦之也。夫聖人之心，施於有政，而布在方冊；其所可見者，治之具也，非其所以治也。惟上智之士，焉能緣法以求心，得心而忘象；反是，而索諸儀章度數者，下也；索諸文字訓詁者，又其下也。甚則臆決懸斷，取聖人之經而亂之。昔人謂漢儒窮經之害慘於秦火，非有所激而云然哉！乃今之亂經者，又不止漢儒巳也。夫自漢惠除挾書之律，孝武建

Shen Jiwen 沈季文

Comment by Associate Examiner and Acting Director (langzhong) Wu 吳: "The Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) is originally a complete work instituted by the Duke of Zhou after governance had been settled, yet readers have thrown it into confusion. This essay traces back to the fundamental origin and judges the intricacies through principle, which is sufficient to dispel the doubts of a thousand ages."
Comment by Associate Examiner and Examining Editor (jiantao) Zhao 趙: "The evidential research is precise and thorough, and the critical argumentation is detailed and incisive. Against the dazzlingly confused and fragmented theories of various scholars, this suffices to serve as the definitive verdict."
Comment by Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting (shidu xueshi) Shen 申: "Learned in antiquity and conversant with the Classics, he judges matters with independent insight—surely a fine scholar. Worthy of inclusion."
Comment by Examiner and Grand Secretary (daxueshi) Zhang 張: "Broadly analytical and possessing special insight, he is indeed a choice scholar of the Classics. Included."

That the sacred Classics are not clear to the world is because those who discourse upon the Classics obscure them. Now, the mind of the Sage was enacted in governance and set forth in written tablets; what can be seen therein are the instruments of governance, not that whereby governance is achieved. Only a scholar of the highest wisdom is able to trace the institutions in order to seek the mind behind them, and upon attaining the mind, forget the outward forms. Conversely, to seek it in ceremonial insignia and numerical measures is inferior; to seek it in textual characters and glosses is lower still. Worse yet are those who make arbitrary decisions and baseless judgments, taking the Classics of the Sage and throwing them into confusion. When people of the past said that the harm done by Han scholars in exhaustively scrutinizing the Classics was more devastating than the fires of Qin, was this not said out of deep provocation! Yet those who throw the Classics into confusion today are not limited merely to the Han scholars. title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
藏書之策齊魯諸儒執經競進傳儀禮者
始於高堂生傳大戴禮者始於瑕丘蕭奮
周禮之書未出也河間獻王得諸李氏而
因以上諸祕府維時學官博士顓門持業
非其師說不稱而謷然求所以相勝一有
異聞隨聲羣詆漢武帝以爲瀆亂不經之
書蓋諸儒之說誤之也自劉歆好之賈鄭
父子習而宗之其說遂稍傳於世至王仲
淹氏曰周禮其敵於天命乎朱仲晦氏曰
===
周官布濩周密乃姬公運用天理之書蓋
至於是而其論始定矣然六官之中惟冬
官缺焉河間獻王補之以考工記取工匠
器械之事與治教政刑躋而並列遂使其

Prince Xian of Hejian obtained it from the Li family and consequently presented it to the Imperial Library. At that time, the Erudites at the official schools specialized in their respective traditions, citing nothing outside their masters' teachings and clamorously seeking to surpass one another; whenever they heard anything different, they echoed each other in collective denunciation. That Emperor Wu of Han considered it a chaotic and uncanonical book was because the theories of these scholars misled him. Once Liu Xin favored it, and the fathers and sons of the Jia and Zheng families studied and revered it, its teachings were gradually transmitted to the world. Coming to Wang Zhongyan [Wang Tong], he said: "Is not the Rites of Zhou equal to the Mandate of Heaven?" And Zhu Zhonghui [Zhu Xi] said: "The Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan) is broadly diffused and thoroughly detailed; it is the book through which the Duke of Zhou put heavenly principle into operation." Only at this point was the assessment of it finally settled. Yet among the six offices, the Office of Winter alone was missing. Prince Xian of Hejian supplemented it with the Record of Trades (Kaogong ji), taking matters of artisans and implements and elevating them to stand alongside governance, instruction, administration, and punishments, which consequently caused the book to be distrusted throughout the realm. Thus scholars of the age ridiculed him, saying: "The one who compromised the Rites of Zhou was Liu De [Prince Xian of Hejian]." Does this not refer to just this? title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
有染人地官有鼓人以至巾車司裘司弓
矢之職秩然具在蓋謂冬官實未嘗亡而
散見於五官之中也澄之爲書麗内史司
士於天官麗大司樂諸子於地官麗封人
牧人於春官麗銜枚司隸於夏官麗司虣
司稽於秋官而縣師廛人等職則以爲冬
官之屬蓋謂五官互見而冬官亦未嘗缺
也主葉氏之說則冬官獨專而五官反殽
主吳氏之說則詮次失倫而意義乖析矧
===
俞廷椿之復古編王次點之訂義丘吉甫
之全書紛紜錯綜莫知所適與之論議其
不爲聚訟者幾希矣此愚之所未解也夫
詩書六藝之敎必折衷於孔氏矣孔氏之
作春秋也終於獲麟距隱桓之世未甚遠
也甲戌己丑夏五紀子伯之訛皆因之而
不改故其言曰多聞闕疑又曰蓋有不知
而作者我無是也六經自秦火以後書亡
四十三篇二雅各亡其六篇於聖人之經

… has the Dyestuff Master (Ranren), and the Offices of Earth (Diguan) has the Drum Master (Guren); extending even to the offices of the Carriage Master (Jinche), Fur Master (Siqiu), and Master of Bows and Arrows (Sigongshi), they are all present in orderly array.” This means that the Offices of Winter (Dongguan) was in fact never lost, but appears scattered throughout the other five offices. In compiling his book, [Wu] Cheng attached the Scribes of the Interior (Neishi) and Directors of Servitors (Sishi) to the Offices of Heaven (Tianguan); attached the Grand Director of Music (Dasile) and Coordinator of Reservoir Sons (Zhuzi) to the Offices of Earth; attached the Boundary Masters (Fengren) and Herdsmen (Muren) to the Offices of Spring (Chunguan); attached the Gag Masters (Xianmei) and Directors of Retainers (Sili) to the Offices of Summer (Xiaguan); and attached the Directors of Turbulence (Sibao) and Directors of Inspection (Siji) to the Offices of Autumn (Qiuguan); whereas offices such as the Masters of Suburban Districts (Xianshi) and Market-Stall Masters (Chanren) he regarded as belonging to the Offices of Winter. This means that the five offices appear interchangeably and the Offices of Winter was likewise never lacking. Yet if one follows the theory of Mr. Ye [Shi], then the Offices of Winter becomes exclusively specialized while the other five offices are instead thrown into confusion; if one follows the theory of Mr. Wu [Cheng], then the sequence loses its proper order and the meaning is perversely fragmented. How much more so with Yu Tingchun’s 俞廷椿 Book of Returning to Antiquity (Fugu bian), Wang Cidian’s 王次點 Emended Meanings (Dingyi), and Qiu Jifu’s 丘吉甫 Complete Book (Quanshu)—tangled and intricate, so that one does not know which way to turn! If one engages in debate with them, how rare it is that it does not turn into a clamorous dispute! This is what I, in my simplicity, fail to understand.

Now, the teachings of the Odes, the Documents, and the Six Arts must be judged by the standard of Confucius. When Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), he ended with the capture of the unicorn, which was not very far removed from the reigns of Dukes Yin and Huan. Yet the textual corruptions of “jiasu and jichou,” “fifth month of summer,” and “Viscount and Earl of Ji” were all left as they were without alteration. title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
則何嘗有所損哉孟氏之言班爵祿曰其
詳不可得而聞也班固之論禮經以為自
孔子時而不具也諸儒生於數千載之下
乃欲掇已去之籍輯煨燼之餘而以己意
為之傅會是其智有加于孔孟也然則聖
人之經終不可明乎蓋聖人之經聖人之
心為之也嘗觀周禮一書纖悉具備自天
官大宰以逮於薙氏柞氏自八典八則以
逮於草木昆蟲品式條貫布濩流行而淵
===
然盎然者實充塞於其間饎羞至瑣也何
與於天官鉅細一也內政至密也何與於
大宰宮府一也馮相保章司天也何與於
春官天人一也遂師司田野也何與於夏
官兵農一也山澤倉庾民所需也何與於
司徒富與教一也當姬公制作之日竭心
思以通於三王其精神貫徹而無所壅閼
其統紀相維而無所隔閡即五官之篇皆
冠之曰體國經野設官分職以為民極極

translation_en: …how did that ever detract from the classics of the sages? When Master Meng (Mencius) spoke of the ranks and emoluments, he said, "The particulars cannot be learned." And when Ban Gu 班固 discussed the Ritual Classics (Lijing 禮經), he held that they were already incomplete in the time of Confucius. Yet the various scholars, born several thousand years later, wish to gather up the records that were already removed and compile the remnants left from the ashes, forcing interpretations upon them according to their own notions—as if their wisdom surpassed that of Confucius and Mencius! If that is so, can the classics of the sages ultimately never be understood? Truly, the classics of the sages are what the minds of the sages produced. I have examined the single book of the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli 周禮), in which every fine detail is complete: from the Grandets/Grand Councilor (Dazai 大宰) in the "Offices of Heaven" (Tianguan 天官) down to the Weed-Clearers (Tishi 薙氏) and Tree-Clearers (Zaoshi 柞氏), and from the Eight Canons (badian 八典) and Eight Rules (baze 八則) down to plants, trees, and insects—its regulations and unifying threads spread everywhere and flow smoothly, while something profound and abundant truly fills the space within it. Cooked food and delicacies are utterly trivial matters; what have they to do with the "Offices of Heaven"? Great and small are one. The administration of the inner palace is utterly private; what has it to do with the Grand Councilor? Palace and government offices are one. The Astrologer (Fengxiang 馮相) and the Astronomer (Baozhang 保章) take charge of the heavens; what have they to do with the "Offices of Spring" (Chunguan 春官)? Heaven and man are one. The Outlying District Master (Suishi 遂師) takes charge of the fields and wilderness; what has he to do with the "Offices of Summer" (Xiaguan 夏官)? Soldiery and agriculture are one. Mountains, marshes, granaries, and storehouses are what the people depend upon; what have they to do with the Minister of Education (Situ 司徒)? Enrichment and instruction are one. On the day when the Duke of Zhou (Jigong 姬公) created these institutions, he exhausted his thoughts to connect with the Three Kings; his spirit penetrated everything without obstruction, and his governing principles bound everything together without division. Even at the head of each of the chapters on the Five Offices, he prefaced them with the words: "It is only the King who establishes the state,辨 [orders] the capital and the countryside, sets up offices, and divides responsibilities, so as to serve as the standard for the people." title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
之爲言中也洪範所謂建其有極者也建
極之義宜專屬於敎典而奚各冠於五官
嗟乎此其義難言矣沉思於度數之外而
冥會於意象之表則冬官雖缺無害也固
不必强爲之解亦不必更置而互易之也
必欲櫛字比句以今人之法而配諸古人
則其鉅者已析之而使二而矧其瑣瑣者
也竊恐侵尋不已全書遂亂是昔之周禮
亡其一而今之周禮亡其六聖經之不明
===
吾不知其所終矣自是書之出習而用之
者何限劉歆著錄略而六幹五均託名於
泉府王介甫訓釋萬餘言而青苗市易藉
口於國服蘇綽用其五六而不足以治周
蘇威用其八九而不足以治隋彼周與隋
循迹而用之猶曰無益於治耳劉歆王安
石窮年矻矻敝其精神於訓詁而卒以其
術禍天下窮經不明之害一至此極乃世
之逞其私說者猶紛紛而未已也可恠也

punctuated: 之爲言中也，《洪範》所謂「建其有極」者也。建極之義，宜專屬於敎典，而奚各冠於五官？嗟乎！此其義難言矣。沉思於度數之外，而冥會於意象之表，則冬官雖缺，無害也，固不必强爲之解，亦不必更置而互易之也。必欲櫛字比句，以今人之法而配諸古人，則其鉅者已析之而使二，而矧其瑣瑣者也？竊恐侵尋不已，全書遂亂，是昔之《周禮》亡其一，而今之《周禮》亡其六。聖經之不明，吾不知其所終矣。自是書之出，習而用之者何限？劉歆著《錄略》，而六幹五均託名於泉府；王介甫訓釋萬餘言，而青苗、市易藉口於國服；蘇綽用其五六，而不足以治周；蘇威用其八九，而不足以治隋。彼周與隋循迹而用之，猶曰無益於治耳；劉歆、王安石窮年矻矻，敝其精神於訓詁，而卒以其術禍天下。窮經不明之害，一至此極，乃世之逞其私說者，猶紛紛而未已也，可恠也！
translation_en:
… means centrality, what the Great Plan (Hongfan) calls "establishing his supreme standard." The principle of establishing the supreme standard ought to belong exclusively to the canon of instruction [the Ministry of Education], so why is it placed at the head of each of the five offices? Alas! The meaning of this is difficult to put into words. If one ponders deeply beyond the mere numbers and regulations and silently apprehends what lies beyond the surface imagery, then even though the Office of Winter (Dongguan) is missing, there is no harm in it. One certainly does not need to force an explanation for it, nor does one need to rearrange and interchange the text. If one insists on combing through every character and matching every phrase, applying the methods of men of today to fit those of the ancients, then even in its grandest aspects one has already split what was one into two—how much more so with the trivial details! I privately fear that if this gradual encroachment does not cease, the entire book will consequently be thrown into disorder; thus the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli) of the past lost one of its six parts, whereas the Rites of Zhou of today will lose all six. With the sacred classic obscured, I do not know where it all will end.

Since this book first appeared, how limitless have been those who studied and applied it! Liu Xin 劉歆 composed his bibliographic summaries (Lulüe), and the "six monopolies" (liugan) and "five equalizations" (wujun) borrowed the name of the Treasury of Currency (Quanfu); Wang Jiefu 王介甫 [Wang Anshi 王安石] wrote commentaries and explanations of over ten thousand words, and his Green Sprouts (qingmiao) and Market Exchange (shiyi) policies used the "state service" (guofu) interest system as a pretext; Su Chuo 蘇綽 applied five or six tenths of it, yet it was insufficient to bring order to the Northern Zhou; Su Wei 蘇威 applied eight or nine tenths of it, yet it was insufficient to bring order to the Sui. When the Zhou and the Sui followed its literal traces and applied it, one could still say it was merely of no benefit to governance. But Liu Xin and Wang Anshi toiled assiduously year after year, exhausting their mental energies on exegetical glosses, only to end up bringing calamity upon the empire with their statecraft. The harm of investigating the classics without true comprehension has reached such an extreme; yet those in the world who indulge their private theories still go on in endless confusion without ceasing. How strange…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
夫今之言學術者必曰黜百家尊孔氏然
莊周斵輪之喻至今學者稱焉顧沿襲口
耳餟聖人之糟粕而又以己意亂之上之
背闕疑之訓下之蹈斵輪之譏其惑也亦
甚矣藉謂愚之言均之臆决然猶就古人
之成書而論之也蓋太史公論帝德帝系
二紀曰總之不離古文者近是而申公之
授詩也疑者則闕而弗傳是孔氏信而好
古之教也
===
第三問
馮夢禎
同考試官都給事中陳批考據詳核品隲精當議論閎博
是有關於世教者宜錄以式
同考試官右贊善陳批儒術勝在本實是作剖析明甚而
詞復古雅非邃養不能
同考試官左諭德陳批俗儒卑卑乃為道法二家所勝論
者亦莫能明其所以然斯文出儒效始章章著矣
考試官侍讀學士申批用二家之所長而脩其本以勝之此儒

punctuated:
夫！今之言學術者，必曰「黜百家，尊孔氏」，然莊周斵輪之喻，至今學者稱焉。顧沿襲口耳，餟聖人之糟粕，而又以己意亂之；上之背闕疑之訓，下之蹈斵輪之譏，其惑也亦甚矣！藉謂愚之言均之臆决，然猶就古人之成書而論之也。蓋太史公論《帝德》、《帝系》二紀曰：「總之不離古文者近是。」而申公之授《詩》也，疑者則闕而弗傳。是孔氏「信而好古」之教也。

第三問
馮夢禎
同考試官都給事中陳批：考據詳核，品隲精當，議論閎博，是有關於世教者，宜錄以式。
同考試官右贊善陳批：儒術勝在本實，是作剖析明甚，而詞復古雅，非邃養不能。
同考試官左諭德陳批：俗儒卑卑，乃為道、法二家所勝，論者亦莫能明其所以然；斯文出，儒效始章章著矣。
考試官侍讀學士申批：用二家之所長，而脩其本以勝之，此儒
translation_en:
…! Those who discuss scholarship today invariably say, "Reject the Hundred Schools and revere only Confucius"; yet Zhuang Zhou's莊周 parable of the wheelwright is still praised by scholars to this day. Instead, they merely pass down hearsay from mouth to ear, feeding on the dregs of the sages while confounding them with their own private notions. Above, they violate the injunction to leave doubtful points aside; below, they invite the wheelwright's ridicule. How profound is their delusion! Even if one were to say that my own humble words are equally based on conjecture, they nevertheless discuss the matter on the basis of the completed texts of the ancients. Indeed, when the Grand Historian (Sima Qian 司馬遷) discussed the two records Imperials Virtues (Dide 帝德) and Imperial Genealogies (Dixi 帝系), he said, "In sum, those who do not depart from the ancient texts are close to the truth." And when Master Shen (Shen Gong 申公) taught the Book of Odes (Shi 詩), where there was doubt he left it blank and did not transmit it. This is Confucius's teaching of "believing in and loving the ancients."

Third Policy Question
Feng Mengzhen 馮夢禎
Associate Examiner Chief Supervising Secretary Chen 陳 comments: The textual research is detailed and exact, the critical evaluations are precise and fitting, and the arguments are broad and learned. This is a piece of import for moral instruction in the world; it should be recorded as a model.
Associate Examiner Right Admonisher Chen 陳 comments: The superiority of Confucianism lies in its fundamental substance. This essay analyzes the matter with utmost clarity, and its diction is moreover antique and elegant—impossible without profound cultivation.
Associate Examiner Left Mentor Chen 陳 comments: Vulgar Confucians are petty and base, and thus are bested by the Daoist and Legalist schools, while commentators have been unable to explain why this is so. With the appearance of this essay, the efficacy of Confucianism is at last made brilliantly manifest.
Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Shen 申 comments: To employ the strengths of the two schools while cultivating one's own fundamental basis in order to surpass them—this is the Confucian…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
者折衷之論是作得之矣宜錄
考試官大學士張批漢儒守章句闇于理道故儒效不見
于世作史者乃右道法而左儒以夷于九流狃所見也揚子之作足破
其謬矣
儒者之于百家衆說非闢之難也有以勝
之之難也夫百家衆說皆持之有故言之
成理足以陳功見能于天下而世之儒者
恒騖于虛聲而不睹于本實卒使天下無
善治而百家衆說顧得挾其所長而勝之
===
嗟乎則豈儒之道端使然哉世無眞儒而
所用非所重也故人主之用儒無爲黃老
申韓所勝則善矣維昔三代之盛道德一
風俗同人無殊言家無異說粹然一出于
正惡睹所謂黃老申韓者蓋聖學之晦久
矣彼見夫澆淳散樸紛華利巧之爲擾也
而絕智棄禮之說出焉彼見夫詭行飾功
浮游夸誕之爲蠹也而明法峻刑之說出
焉蓋可以成一家之言而不可以通萬方

punctuated:
者折衷之論，是作得之矣，宜錄。
考試官大學士張批：漢儒守章句，闇于理道，故儒效不見于世。作史者乃右道、法而左儒，以夷于九流，狃所見也。揚子之作，足破其謬矣。
儒者之于百家衆說，非闢之難也，有以勝之之難也。夫百家衆說，皆持之有故，言之成理，足以陳功見能于天下。而世之儒者，恒騖于虛聲，而不睹于本實，卒使天下無善治，而百家衆說顧得挾其所長而勝之。嗟乎！則豈儒之道端使然哉？世無眞儒，而所用非所重也。故人主之用儒，無爲黃、老、申、韓所勝，則善矣。維昔三代之盛，道德一，風俗同，人無殊言，家無異說，粹然一出于正，惡睹所謂黃、老、申、韓者？蓋聖學之晦久矣。彼見夫澆淳散樸、紛華利巧之爲擾也，而絕智棄禮之說出焉；彼見夫詭行飾功、浮游夸誕之爲蠹也，而明法峻刑之說出焉。蓋可以成一家之言，而不可以通萬方…
translation_en:
… balanced discourse of a Confucian scholar; this essay has grasped it and ought to be recorded.
Examiner and Grand Secretary Zhang comments: The Confucian scholars of the Han dynasty clung to chapter-and-verse exegesis and were benighted regarding the principles of governance; hence the efficacy of Confucianism was not manifest in the world. Writers of history therefore elevated the Daoist and Legalist schools above the Confucians, reducing the latter to the level of the Nine Schools, simply out of habit from what they had witnessed. This piece by Master Yang [or: this essay on Master Yang] is sufficient to shatter their fallacy.
In a Confucian scholar's engagement with the myriad doctrines of the Hundred Schools, the difficulty lies not in refuting them, but in possessing the means to prevail over them. Now, the myriad doctrines of the Hundred Schools all have grounds for what they maintain and form coherent arguments in what they say, sufficient to display achievements and demonstrate capabilities throughout the empire. Yet the Confucians of the age constantly chase after empty reputation without attending to fundamental substance. In the end, they leave the empire without good governance, while the myriad doctrines of the Hundred Schools are instead able to leverage their strengths and prevail over them. Alas! Could it really be the Way of the Confucians that causes things to be so? It is rather that the age lacks true Confucians, and what is employed is not what ought to be valued. Therefore, when a ruler employs Confucians, if he ensures they are not prevailed over by the followers of Huang-Lao [the Yellow Emperor and Laozi] and Shen-Han [Shen Buhai and Han Fei], then all will be well. In the flourishing era of the Three Dynasties of antiquity, morality was unified and customs were uniform; people had no divergent words and families held no heterodox doctrines. Everything issued purely from orthodoxy—where could one have seen the so-called followers of Huang-Lao or Shen-Han? Indeed, the learning of the sages had been obscured for a long time. When those thinkers saw how the watering down of purity, the scattering of simplicity, and the pursuit of ostentatious splendor and clever profit caused turmoil, the doctrine of abandoning wisdom and discarding ritual arose. When those others saw how deceitful conduct, fabricated merit, and rootless, boastful extravagance acted as a pestilence, the doctrine of clear laws and harsh punishments arose. Such teachings can form the doctrine of a single school, yet cannot serve as a comprehensive strategy for all regions…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
之略可以救一時之敝而不可以定萬世
之經也儒者睹其指而憂其害則常辭而
闢之雖然習之者不知其非而闢之者不
得其術吾未見其能勝也夫天下不患有
黃老申韓而患無儒儒之貴于黃老申韓
也非以名勝之而貴其實也非以末勝之
而貴其本也儒者不脩其實不務其本徒
舉而加諸黃老申韓之上曰儒求所以爲
儒者而實非也則是以助之之說勝之也
===
夫惟察黃老申韓之短長究世儒之得失
然後可以明道術而達治體矣今夫黃老
之失使人獨任清虛蕩檢踰節其事難以
徧循然而立俗施事合大道之因秉要執
本得南面之術則百家不能易也申韓之
失使人務于慘刻傷恩薄厚其計不可長
用然而尊主卑臣足以明分職信賞必罰
足以輔禮制則百家不能改也此黃老申
韓之所長而史談班固之所予也乃若博

punctuated: 之略；可以救一時之敝，而不可以定萬世之經也。儒者睹其指而憂其害，則常辭而闢之。雖然，習之者不知其非，而闢之者不得其術，吾未見其能勝也。夫天下不患有黃老、申韓，而患無儒。儒之貴于黃老、申韓也，非以名勝之，而貴其實也；非以末勝之，而貴其本也。儒者不脩其實，不務其本，徒舉而加諸黃老、申韓之上曰「儒」，求所以爲儒者而實非也，則是以助之之說勝之也。夫惟察黃老、申韓之短長，究世儒之得失，然後可以明道術而達治體矣。今夫黃老之失，使人獨任清虛，蕩檢踰節，其事難以徧循；然而立俗施事，合大道之因，秉要執本，得南面之術，則百家不能易也。申韓之失，使人務于慘刻，傷恩薄厚，其計不可長用；然而尊主卑臣，足以明分職，信賞必罰，足以輔禮制，則百家不能改也。此黃老、申韓之所長，而史談、班固之所予也。乃若博
translation_en: …governance; they can remedy the abuses of a single moment, yet cannot establish the constant standard for ten thousand generations. When Confucians observe their purport and worry about the harm they cause, they constantly speak out to refute them. Even so, those who practice these teachings do not realize they are wrong, while those who refute them fail to grasp the proper method; I have yet to see that the latter are able to prevail. Indeed, the world need not worry that there are devotees of Huang-Lao and of Shen Buhai and Han Fei, but rather that there are no true Confucians. What makes Confucians superior to Huang-Lao and to Shen and Han is not that they prevail over them in name, but that they value substance; not that they prevail over them in secondary matters, but that they value the fundamental. When Confucians do not cultivate their substance or attend to their fundamentals, and merely elevate themselves above Huang-Lao and Shen and Han by calling themselves "Confucians," if one seeks what actually makes them Confucians and finds that in reality they are not, then they are trying to prevail over those teachings with arguments that actually aid them. Only by examining the shortcomings and strengths of Huang-Lao and of Shen and Han, and investigating the successes and failures of the Confucians of the age, can one clarify the Way and its methods and comprehend the principles of governance. Now, the failing of Huang-Lao is that it causes men to rely solely on pure emptiness, casting aside restraint and overstepping proper bounds, so that its practices are difficult to follow universally; yet in establishing customs and administering affairs, it accords with the natural responsiveness of the Great Way, and in holding to essentials and grasping fundamentals, it attains the art of ruling as a sovereign facing south—this none of the Hundred Schools can alter. The failing of Shen and Han is that it causes men to devote themselves to harshness and severity, injuring kindness and diminishing generosity, so that its schemes cannot be employed for long; yet in exalting the ruler and subordinating the ministers, it suffices to clarify the division of offices, and in making rewards trustworthy and punishments certain, it suffices to assist ritual institutions—this none of the Hundred Schools can change. These are the strengths of Huang-Lao and of Shen and Han, and what Grand Scribe Sima Tan 司馬談 and Ban Gu 班固 praised. As for being broad in learning…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
而寡要勞而罔功惑者旣失精微而辟者
又離道本則儒者之失而史談班固之所
譏也黃老申韓之所長如彼儒者之失若
此欲以相勝不亦難乎愚請略陳漢事得
失之效當干戈甫定庠序未遑非休養生
息時耶文帝乃下寬大之詔脩玄默之化
破觚爲圓斲雕爲樸于是風移俗易庶幾
成康刑措之隆此善用黃老之效也乃武
帝之用儒則舛矣承明侍從持論不根徒
===
步公卿曲學阿世聞力行之言則報罷陳
天人之策而見疏卽黜百家尊孔氏特具
文耳彼好大喜功紛更多事則不逮文帝
遠矣其弊也海內虛耗幾續秦亡武帝固
有以致之歟當官職廢弛閭閻怨咨此非
總攬振刷時耶宣帝乃明法審令循名核
實樞機周愼品式詳明卒之吏稱民安庶
幾周宣中興之烈此善用申韓之效也乃
元帝之用儒則陋矣牢賈五鹿以巧佞梁

息時耶文帝乃下寬大之詔脩玄默之化
破觚爲圜斵雕爲樸于是風移俗易庶幾
成康刑措之隆此善用黃老之效也乃武
帝之用儒則舛矣承明侍從持論不根徒
===
步公卿曲學阿世聞力行之言則報罷陳
天人之策而見疏卽黜百家尊孔氏特具
文耳彼好大喜功紛更多事則不逮文帝
遠矣其蔽也海內虛耗幾續秦亡武帝固
有以致之歟當官職廢弛闒闒怨咨此非
總攬振刷時耶宣帝乃明法審令循名核
實樞機周愼品式詳明卒之吏稱民安庶
幾周宣中興之烈此善用申韓之效也乃
元帝之用儒則陋矣牢貫五鹿以巧佞求
punctuated: 而寡要，勞而罔功，惑者旣失精微，而辟者又離道本，則儒者之失，而史談、班固之所譏也。黃老、申韓之所長如彼，儒者之失若此，欲以相勝，不亦難乎？愚請略陳漢事得失之效：當干戈甫定，庠序未遑，非休養生息時耶？文帝乃下寬大之詔，脩玄默之化，破觚爲圓，斲雕爲樸，于是風移俗易，庶幾成、康刑措之隆，此善用黃老之效也。乃武帝之用儒則舛矣。承明侍從，持論不根；徒步公卿，曲學阿世。聞力行之言則報罷，陳天人之策而見疏，卽黜百家、尊孔氏，特具文耳。彼好大喜功，紛更多事，則不逮文帝遠矣。其弊也，海內虛耗，幾續秦亡，武帝固有以致之歟？當官職廢弛，閭閻怨咨，此非總攬振刷時耶？宣帝乃明法審令，循名核實，樞機周愼，品式詳明，卒之吏稱民安，庶幾周宣中興之烈，此善用申韓之效也。乃元帝之用儒則陋矣。牢、賈、五鹿以巧佞梁
translation_en: … yet lacking in essentials, laborious yet achieving no merit; the deluded lose sight of subtle profundities, while the biased depart from the fundamental Way—these are the failings of the Confucians, which Grand Scribe Tan (Sima Tan 司馬談) and Ban Gu 班固 criticized. Since the strengths of Huang-Lao and of Shen Buhai 申不害 and Han Fei 韓非 are like that, and the failings of the Confucians are like this, if one wishes the latter to prevail over the former, is it not difficult? I beg to briefly set forth the effects of successes and failures in the affairs of the Han dynasty. When warfare had just been settled and there was not yet leisure for schools, was this not the time for resting and nurturing the people? Emperor Wen 文帝 accordingly issued magnanimous edicts and cultivated transforming influence through mysterious quietude, rounding off sharp corners and carving away ornate decoration into simplicity. Thereupon customs and morals were transformed, nearly matching the flourishing era of Kings Cheng 成王 and Kang 康王 when punishments were set aside—this was the effect of skillfully employing Huang-Lao. Yet Emperor Wu's 武帝 employment of Confucians went awry. The attendants in the Chengming 承明殿 Court held forth with unfounded arguments, while those who rose on foot from commoner status to the Three Dukes and Nine Ministers twisted their learning to flatter the age. When he heard words advocating strenuous practice of virtue, he dismissed them; when the policy essays on Heaven and Humanity were presented, their author was kept at a distance. Even his dismissing of the Hundred Schools and venerating of Confucius was merely an empty formality. In his fondness for grandiose achievements and his disorderly changing of institutions and multiplying of affairs, he fell far short of Emperor Wen. As for the resulting abuses, the realm within the seas was exhausted and depleted, nearly repeating the fall of Qin—did Emperor Wu not indeed bring this about himself? When official duties had fallen into neglect and the common people in the lanes and alleys murmured in resentment, was this not the time for gathering overall control and invigorating administration? Emperor Xuan 宣帝 accordingly clarified the laws and examined ordinances, demanding that realities match titles; the central pivot of government was thorough and cautious, and regulations and standards were detailed and clear. In the end, officials were competent and the people were at peace, nearly matching the illustrious restoration of King Xuan of Zhou 周宣王—this was the effect of skillfully employing Shen Buhai and Han Fei. Yet Emperor Yuan's 元帝 employment of Confucians was base. Lao Liang 牢梁, Jia Juanzhi 賈捐之 [?], and Wulu Chongzong 五鹿充宗 through artful flattery [?]…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
容貢薛韋匡以循默守位師傅自裁于請
室權奸得肆于憑城即徵用儒生委之政
事特虛聲耳彼牽制舊文優游寡斷則不
及宣帝明矣其弊也政柄潛移終衰漢業
元帝固有以取之歟夫以武帝之儒當文
帝之黃老其數不勝也以元帝之儒當宣
帝之申韓其數不勝也何者彼無欲自化
清靜自正而吾猶利祿之陋習也彼以言
責事以事責功而吾猶章句之空談也故
===
黃老申韓之得行其說則世儒之罪也觀
者見其然乃曰雖有美種不如荑稗之熟
雖有儒術不如他道之成是輿羽鈞金之
謂耳豈不易之論哉蓋古今之言儒者折
衷于周孔周公諭敎成王歌雍詠勺而天
下安致辟管蔡破斧缺斨而天下服孔子
勝殘去殺則以稱善人誅卯隳都則以治
魯國蓋言仁必言義而萬世之道術祖之
言猛必言寬而萬世之治體因之是儒之

言猛必言寬而萬世之治體因之是儒之
punctuated: 容，貢、薛、韋、匡以循默守位，師傅自裁于請室，權奸得肆于憑城。即徵用儒生，委之政事，特虛聲耳。彼牽制舊文，優游寡斷，則不及宣帝明矣。其弊也，政柄潛移，終衰漢業，元帝固有以取之歟？夫以武帝之儒當文帝之黃老，其數不勝也；以元帝之儒當宣帝之申韓，其數不勝也。何者？彼無欲自化，清靜自正，而吾猶利祿之陋習也；彼以言責事，以事責功，而吾猶章句之空談也。故黃老、申韓之得行其說，則世儒之罪也。觀者見其然，乃曰：「雖有美種，不如荑稗之熟；雖有儒術，不如他道之成。」是輿羽鈞金之謂耳，豈不易之論哉？蓋古今之言儒者，折衷于周、孔。周公諭敎成王，歌《雍》詠《勺》而天下安；致辟管、蔡，破斧缺斨而天下服。孔子勝殘去殺，則以稱善人；誅卯隳都，則以治魯國。蓋言仁必言義，而萬世之道術祖之；言猛必言寬，而萬世之治體因之。是儒之
translation_en: … [accommodated] by artful flattery; Gong Yu, Xue Guangde, Wei Xuancheng, and Kuang Heng held onto their positions through compliance and silence; his Grand Tutor [Xiao Wangzhi] took his own life in the prison for officials, while powerful villains ran rampant like foxes relying on a city wall. Even though he summoned and employed Confucian scholars and entrusted them with governance, this was merely empty reputation. Bound by old texts, hesitant and indecisive, he was clearly inferior to Emperor Xuan. As for the resulting abuses, the reins of government secretly shifted, ultimately causing the decline of the Han enterprise—did not Emperor Yuan indeed bring this upon himself? Now, when the Confucianism of Emperor Wu is matched against the Huang-Lao of Emperor Wen, in practical effect it cannot prevail; when the Confucianism of Emperor Yuan is matched against the Shen Buhai and Han Fei Legalism of Emperor Xuan, in practical effect it cannot prevail. Why is this? Because those doctrines achieved spontaneous transformation through desirelessness and spontaneous rectitude through tranquility, whereas ours remained stuck in the vulgar habit of seeking profit and emolument; those doctrines demanded deeds from words and results from deeds, whereas ours remained stuck in the empty talk of chapter-and-verse exegesis. Therefore, that the doctrines of Huang-Lao and of Shen and Han were able to prevail is the fault of the vulgar Confucians of the age. Observers, seeing this, thereupon say: "Though there may be fine grain, it is not as good as tares and barnyard grass when they are ripe; though there exists the Confucian art, it is not as good as other ways when they achieve results." This is like comparing a cartload of feathers to a jun of gold—how could it be an immutable argument? Indeed, discussions of Confucianism past and present find their ultimate standard in the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. When the Duke of Zhou instructed and guided King Cheng, singing the "Yong" and chanting the "Shao" odes, all under Heaven was at peace; when he executed Guan Shu and Cai Shu, breaking axes and chipping hatchets, all under Heaven submitted. Confucius spoke of overcoming cruelty and eliminating capital punishment when praising "good men"; yet he executed Shaozheng Mao and dismantled the fortified cities when governing the state of Lu. For when speaking of benevolence, they invariably spoke of righteousness, and the philosophical arts of ten thousand generations take them as their ancestor; when speaking of severity, they invariably spoke of leniency, and the governing principles of ten thousand generations follow upon them. This is the… [main thread] of Confucianism…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
本統而黄老申韓之所不能抗也後之儒
者吾惑焉逢衣淺帶禹行舜趨愼容節而
忽檢柙命之曰賤儒墨守訓故緣飾章采
崇論竑議而不睹其指歸命之曰陋儒拘
攣局曲抱咫尺之義略法先王而足亂世
術命之曰俗儒飾藝文奸譁衆取寵詭故
而不近于情艱言而不中其實命之曰僞
儒四儒者出而人主持以名高之議論蠭
起莫知所定不入于紛亂則入于因循而
===
===
三代之治終不可復睹則漢之武帝元帝
是矣又何以責黄老申韓也然則世無周
孔是黄老申韓者終不可勝乎曰明周孔
之道以勝之彼以清靜吾當之以仁以寛
之說而納之制度名檢以救其偏彼以法
術吾當之以義以猛之說而歸之忠信愛
利以維其敝是黄老申韓者能爲吾用而
不能爲吾害也時張而張時弛而弛明仁
義之用適寛猛之宜以救一時之敝而便

punctuated: 本統，而黄、老、申、韓之所不能抗也。後之儒者，吾惑焉。逢衣淺帶，禹行舜趨，愼容節而忽檢柙，命之曰「賤儒」；墨守訓故，緣飾章采，崇論竑議而不睹其指歸，命之曰「陋儒」；拘攣局曲，抱咫尺之義，略法先王而足亂世術，命之曰「俗儒」；飾藝文奸，譁衆取寵，詭故而不近于情，艱言而不中其實，命之曰「僞儒」。四儒者出，而人主持以名高之，議論蠭起，莫知所定，不入于紛亂，則入于因循，而三代之治終不可復睹，則漢之武帝、元帝是矣，又何以責黄、老、申、韓也？然則世無周、孔，是黄、老、申、韓者終不可勝乎？曰：明周、孔之道以勝之。彼以清靜，吾當之以仁、以寛之說，而納之制度名檢以救其偏；彼以法術，吾當之以義、以猛之說，而歸之忠信愛利以維其敝。是黄、老、申、韓者，能爲吾用而不能爲吾害也。時張而張，時弛而弛，明仁義之用，適寛猛之宜，以救一時之敝而便
translation_en: …fundamental orthodoxy of the Confucians, which Huang-Lao and Shen-Han cannot rival. As for the Confucians of later ages, I am perplexed by them. Wearing voluminous robes and narrow sashes, walking like Yu and hastening like Shun, careful about deportment and etiquette yet neglectful of moral restraint—these may be called "base Confucians." Blindly clinging to glosses and commentaries, embellishing with literary flair, engaging in lofty discourses and grand debates without seeing their ultimate purport—these may be called "narrow Confucians." Cramped and parochial, clutching at petty principles, superficially modeling themselves on the former kings while doing enough tothrow the statecraft of the age into confusion—these may be called "vulgar Confucians." Adorning their arts to gloss over wickedness, sensationalizing to curry favor with the crowd, contriving novelties far removed from human nature, and uttering abstruse words that miss the reality—these may be called "false Confucians." When these four types of Confucians emerge and the ruler upholds them for their high reputation, debates swarm uplike bees and no one knows what to settle upon. Governance either falls into tumultuous confusion or sinks into passive routine, so that the order of the Three Dynasties can never be seen again—such was the case with Emperor Wu and Emperor Yuan of the Han. How then can one blame Huang-Lao and Shen-Han? Well then, if the world lacks a Duke of Zhou or a Confucius, can Huang-Lao and Shen-Han ultimately never be overcome? I say: illuminate the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius to overcome them. Where they advocate tranquility and quiescence, we match them with our doctrines of benevolence and leniency, while channeling them into institutions, names, and standards to remedy their one-sidedness. Where they advocate law and statecraft, we match them with our doctrines of righteousness and severity, while grounding them in loyalty, trustworthiness, love, and benefit to redress their abuses. Thus Huang-Lao and Shen-Han can be put to our use and cannot do us harm. Tightening when it is time to tighten, relaxing when it is time to relax, illuminating the application of benevolence and righteousness, and fitting the proper measure of leniency and severity, so as to remedy the abuses of a single era and bring convenience…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
于民以定萬世之經而適于治是使天下
取足于儒者之道而無待于黃老申韓之
說也彼為其說者如爝火之當大明難為
熾矣是惡能勝儒而亦惡用闢之嗟乎非
明道術達治體者不足以語此是愚生之
所能言而未之逮也
第四問
俞霑

于民，以定萬世之經而適于治。是使天下取足于儒者之道，而無待于黃老、申韓之說也。彼為其說者，如爝火之當大明，難為熾矣。是惡能勝儒，而亦惡用闢之？嗟乎！非明道術、達治體者，不足以語此。是愚生之所能言，而未之逮也。

第四問
俞霑

考試官侍讀學士申批：〔論文體、學術，能根極弊源及還雅道，〕
translation_en:
… to the people, and to establish the constant standard for ten thousand generations so as to be suited to good governance. This is to cause the world to find sufficiency in the Way of the Confucians, without having to rely upon the doctrines of Huang-Lao or Shen Buhai and Han Fei. Those who advocate their doctrines are like torch-fires facing the great brightness of the sun and moon—it is hard for them to blaze! How then could they prevail over the Confucians, and what need is there to refute them? Alas! With anyone who does not illuminate the art of the Way and comprehend the essentials of governance, one cannot speak of this. This is what this foolish student is able to put into words, though I have not yet reached it in practice.

Yu Zhan

Moreover, the page is filled with elegant diction sufficient to wash away vulgar habits; it should be recorded as a model.]

Comment by Examiner Hanlin Reader-in-Waiting Academician Shen: [In discussing literary style and scholarly learning, he is able to trace the root source of the abuses and the way to return to elegance…]

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
不當以文士目之
考試官大學士張批〔原今日文敝由學者不務窮經而叛〕
叛經可謂根極之論錄之用爲上督敞焉
文章之體何其洋洋纚纚愈趨而愈無窮
也始朴矣必流而爲華旣華矣必溢而爲
勝文至于勝則藻繢具而純白傷剞劂施
而矩矱戾天下方以奇靡相馳逐而不知
淳質微缺卒之淪雅道而播其頹風也憂
世之士蓋懍懍焉彼以元化稱者曰文章
===
汚隆與時高下故氣激而唱者自鳴響至
而赴者畢會一神理自然之證人力胡能
與也以世教稱者曰射以的中文以摹成
故招之者一人而應呼則聲沸挽之者亦
一人而競趨則行改轉移化導之力在人
而不在天也愚謂文非風氣無以開其源
非聖哲無以遏其流之二者常相待也迺
其維風起敝宰握化權則人之力勝矣蓋
嘗觀一代開創之初敦龐純固之氣始出

translation_en:
…one ought not to regard him merely as a man of letters.
Examiner and Grand Secretary Zhang's comment: 〔Tracing the corruption of literary style today to scholars failing to devote themselves to exhausting the Classics, and rebelling against [the Ancestral Way and]〕 rebelling against the Classics—this may truly be called an argument that reaches the very root. We record it here to serve as a warning and encouragement for scholars [?].

How vast, flowing, and continuous are the forms of literary composition, growing ever more boundless the further they develop! In the beginning they are unadorned, yet they inevitably flow into华 (ornamentation); once ornate, they inevitably overflow into excess. When writing reaches the point of excess, embellished patterns are complete while pure simplicity is marred; the carver's chisel is applied while the standard rules are violated. The world is just then racing after one another in pursuit of the strange and extravagant, unaware that pure substance is subtly waning, until in the end the refined Way is submerged and decadent customs are spread abroad. Scholars who worry for the world are indeed filled with apprehension over this. Those who explain it in terms of primordial transformation say: "The decline and flourishing of literature rise and fall with the times. Thus, when the vital ethos is stirred, those who lead the chant sing out of themselves; when the echo arrives, those who hasten to it all gather together. It is entirely a manifestation of the natural workings of spiritual principle—how could human effort take part in it?" Those who explain it in terms of worldly instruction say: "Archery hits the mark by means of a target; literature is brought to completion by means of imitation. Thus, though the one who beckons is a single person, those who answer the call make a clamor of voices; though the one who pulls back is also a single person, those who vie to follow change their course. The power to shift, transform, and guide lies with man and not with Heaven." In my humble view, without the prevailing ethos of the times, literature has no means to open its source; without sages and worthies, it has no means to stem its flow. These two always depend upon each other; yet when it comes to upholding customs, remedying abuses, and holding the authority of transformation, human effort prevails. Indeed, I have observed that at the founding of a dynasty, a thick, substantial, pure, and solid vital氣 (energy) first emerges…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
而不勝其蓄故人皆質木而其文渾厚
雅與國風同其冲融睎之有餘光咀之有
遺味焉中葉以後蓄者日詘于出于是巧
慧扇熾而文人學子始掇華獵豔以相誇
詡高者入于玄眇而瑰異倔奇卑者工于
鉤棘而詰曲亢厲理本易簡而綴以悠謬
之詞事涉徑省而伸以羡漫之語文體蓋
日趨于敝矣夫文非末技也據經翼傳所
以統聖真也矢謨陳烈所以裨國是也敷
===
言垂訓所以齊民志也其醇醨華實寔關
世道之盛衰故文敝而世道從之矣自昔
好古君子目擊時弊則必力起而維之用
以剟僞爲真反刓爲樸彼其心誠爲世道
計而直謂造化之權在我已試以韓歐二
氏徵之昔唐承五季綺麗之餘文盛質窮
氣象日萎荼矣乃韓愈刋落陳言本以六
經而八代之頹風丕振功何偉也宋嘉祐
時文體趨于險恠太學之士爭慕效矣歐

translation_en:
…is not outweighed by what has been stored within. Thus people are all simple and unadorned, and their writing is rich, substantial, and refined, sharing the same harmonious blend as the customs of the state; gazing upon it, there is a lingering brilliance, and savoring it, there is an enduring flavor. From the mid-dynasty onward, what has been stored up is increasingly exhausted by what is poured forth. Thereupon, cleverness and wit fan into a blaze, and literati and scholars begin to pluck ornate blossoms and hunt for flashy beauties to boast to one another. The lofty among them enter into abstruse subtleties, becoming bizarre and eccentric; the lowly among them specialize in thorny intricacy, becoming convoluted and strident. Where the principle is originally easy and simple, they patch it with far-fetched and absurd verbiage; where the matter is straightforward and brief, they stretch it out with diffuse and extravagant language. Literary style thus daily tends toward corruption.

Now, writing is no trivial craft: basing oneself on the Classics and supporting the commentaries is the means to unify the true teachings of the sages; setting forth counsels and displaying meritorious deeds is the means to aid the policies of the state; spreading words and handing down instructions is the means to align the minds of the people. Whether it is pure or thin,华 (flowery) or substantial, truly bears upon the flourishing or decline of the moral order of the world; therefore, when writing becomes corrupted, the moral order of the world follows it. Since antiquity, whenever gentlemen who loved the ancient ways witnessed the abuses of their times, they would invariably rise up with all their strength to sustain and restore it, thereby paring away falsehood to make way for truth and returning what was worn smooth back to uncarved simplicity. In their hearts they were genuinely planning for the moral order of the world, and squarely held that the power of transformative creation rested with themselves alone.

Let us test this by examining the two masters Han [Yu] and Ouyang [Xiu]. In former times, the Tang inherited the ornate and florid remnants of the preceding five dynasties; ornament flourished while substance was exhausted, and the prevailing spirit daily withered away. Then Han Yu 韓愈 pared away stale clichés, grounded his writing in the Six Classics, and grandly revitalized the decadent customs of eight dynasties—how magnificent was his achievement! During the Jiayou 嘉祐 era (1056–1063) of the Song, literary style tended toward theperverse and strange, and the scholars of the Imperial University (Taixue) vied in admiring and imitating it. title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
陽脩一排抑之而囂薄遂以釐革効何捷
也蓋由今觀韓氏之文奧衍閎深粹然一
出于正原道原性諸篇論者謂其周情孔
思與孟軻揚雄相表裏歐陽氏之學推韓
孟以達於孔氏其言簡而明信而通引物
連類歸于理奧眉山蘇氏所亟稱豔羡者
也彼二君子者當流敝衡决之日欲障狂
瀾而東之而以其身為之倡譬之竽先而
眾樂和標植而羣足趨未有倡之不應者
===
也謂文與時敝而諉諸氣運之不可返也
豈得為通論哉我
國家洪永之世闢草昧而經綸之神初晰而
光未吐也一時文章皆醇茂款直不競于
華宣成相承殷阜登而徽烈洊奮矣然文
尚束于教斤斤然先民之程度蘊崇以至
弘治則文物濬發而光藻舄奕于天下士
皆遴稱上世之業而卑疵晚近為不及格
矣比嘉靖間作者逾沛艾而起炳烺至今

translation_en:
…[Ouyang] Xiu 歐陽脩 rejected and suppressed them at a single stroke, and the noisy, superficial style was thereby reformed—how swift was the effect! Indeed, when we examine Mr. Han's [Han Yu's 韓愈] writings today, they are abstruse, expansive, vast, and profound, purely issuing from orthodoxy. Of such pieces as his "On the Way" (Yuan Dao 原道) and "On Human Nature" (Yuan Xing 原性), critics say they embody the sentiments of the Duke of Zhou and the thoughts of Confucius, standing as the complement to Meng Ke 孟軻 [Mencius] and Yang Xiong 揚雄. The learning of Mr. Ouyang traced Han [Yu] and Meng [Ke] back to reach Confucius; his words are concise yet clear, trustworthy yet comprehensive, drawing analogies and connecting categories to return to the depths of principle—that which Mr. Su 蘇氏 of Meishan 眉山 [Su Shi 蘇軾] repeatedly praised and admired. Those two gentlemen, in a day when degenerate trends burst their banks, wished to dam the raging waves and turn them eastward, taking the lead in their own persons. It was like the yu-pipes leading and all the other musical instruments harmonizing, or a signpost being erected and the feet of the multitude hastening toward it; never has someone taken the lead without others responding. To say that literature deteriorates along with the times and to blame it on an irreversible cycle of fate—how can that be considered a sound judgment!

In our dynasty, during the Hongwu 洪武 (1368–1398) and Yongle 永樂 (1403–1424) eras, the realm was opened up out of primeval chaos and set in order; its spirit had just grown clear, yet its radiance had not been fully discharged. The writings of that age were all pure, flourishing, sincere, and direct, not competing in華 [florid ornament]. The Xuande 宣德 (1426–1435) and Chenghua 成化 (1465–1487) eras succeeded one another, when abundance and prosperity ascended and fine achievements repeatedly surged forth; yet literature remained bound by instruction, scrupulously adhering to the standards of the ancients. Accumulating and building up until the Hongzhi 弘治 era (1488–1505), cultural accomplishments burst forth deeply, and brilliant literary elegance shone resplendently throughout the empire. Scholars all selectively praised the works of high antiquity and disdained the recent past as failing to meet the standard. By the Jiajing 嘉靖 era (1522–1566), authors rose up with ever greater vigor and grandeur, shining brightly down to the present…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
於乎盛哉乃論者竊咨咨有過計也曰文
體昔嘗典實矣今也託釀郁以肆其澶漫
依閎博以逞其虛恢甚之舍肯綮而談末
緒工外飾而寡真核者比比也昔嘗平正
矣今也意必索于入微詞必期于創獲神
施鬼設駭目洞心而後稱雕蔚也茲二者
文勝之弊反之不可不亟也乃其弊端則
微矣夫文體之于學術固本原而支委也
學務本實則文雖菽粟布帛而充然有餘
===
適一務于華則極之繡鼙帨飾銀黃猶搰
搰焉用力弗已也今六籍之訓昭如日星
非古今所謂至文乎自制科持此為先資
而佔畢之徒猥以陳言目之故字比句櫛
為綴文計耳微旨精義何知探索而亦何
發明之有語訓詁則謝漢之師承語造詣
則謝宋之實踐而經學直土梗矣此不務
窮經之敝也諸子百家持論未可盡絀要
之小已不足以齊大雅今乃剽其洸洋以

punctuated: 於乎盛哉！乃論者竊咨咨有過計也，曰：「文體昔嘗典實矣，今也託釀郁以肆其澶漫，依閎博以逞其虛恢；甚之舍肯綮而談末緒，工外飾而寡真核者，比比也。昔嘗平正矣，今也意必索于入微，詞必期于創獲，神施鬼設，駭目洞心，而後稱雕蔚也。茲二者，文勝之弊，反之不可不亟也。」乃其弊端則微矣。夫文體之于學術，固本原而支委也。學務本實，則文雖菽粟布帛，而充然有餘適；一務于華，則極之繡鼙帨、飾銀黃，猶搰搰焉用力弗已也。今六籍之訓，昭如日星，非古今所謂至文乎？自制科持此為先資，而佔畢之徒猥以陳言目之，故字比句櫛，為綴文計耳。微旨精義，何知探索，而亦何發明之有？語訓詁則謝漢之師承，語造詣則謝宋之實踐，而經學直土梗矣。此不務窮經之敝也。諸子百家，持論未可盡絀，要之小已，不足以齊大雅。今乃剽其洸洋以
translation_en:
…Oh, how flourishing! Yet critics privately sigh and harbor anxious concerns, saying: "Literary style was once classical and substantial; now, under the pretext of rich depth, writers indulge in rambling extravagance, and leaning on vast erudition, they show off hollow grandiloquence. Worse still, those who abandon the essential crux to discuss trivial threads, or who excel at outward ornament while lacking true substance, are everywhere. Style was once balanced and upright; now, ideas must be sought in the most minute subtleties, and phrasing must aim for novel invention. Only when deployed with supernatural cunning to startle the eye and pierce the heart is it praised as finely wrought and luxuriant. These two tendencies are the ills of literary excess, and turning back from them is an urgent necessity."

Yet the root of these ills is subtle. Literary style in relation to scholarly learning is fundamentally a matter of root and branch, source and stream. When learning is devoted to fundamental substance, even if the writing is as plain as beans, grain, and homespun cloth, it is amply satisfying. Once devoted to华丽 (superficial華/ornament), even if taken to the extreme of embroidering leather belts and sashes or adorning with silver and gold, people still toil away relentlessly without end. Now, the teachings of the Six Classics shine as brightly as the sun and stars—are they not what past and present call the ultimate literature? Ever since the civil service examinations took them as the primary stepping-stone, merememorizers of texts have vulgarly regarded them as stale clichés. Thus, they align words and comb through sentences merely as a scheme for piecing together essays. As for their subtle purport and refined meaning, what do they know of exploring them, and what elucidation could there possibly be? Speak of exegesis, and they fall short of the master-disciple transmissions of the Han; speak of personal attainment, and they fall short of the practical cultivation of the Song—so that classical learning has become nothing more than a clay puppet. This is the ill of not striving to exhaust the Classics.

As for the arguments maintained by the Various Masters and Hundred Schools, they cannot be entirely dismissed, but in sum they are minor and insufficient to equal the great standard of elegance. Now, however, people plagiarize their sweeping, unbridled rhetoric in order to…

punctuated: □趣，拾其俶詭以為詞；論道德必援玄虛，議經濟必參法術，而視六籍反蔑如也。此敢于叛經之敝也。蓋學術日頗而文體愈敝，其錮於人心非一朝一夕矣。即有韓、歐二君子者出而推挽於其間，彼且溺舊業為嚆矢，薄正論為巵言，羣詆而竊笑之也。此可以空言化導哉？昔人有云：「士之愛名，如水之就下；上有好者，下必甚焉。」故民之從上也以令，士之象上也以指。一朴愿售，則浮胥化而為雅；一巧偽售，則雅胥化而為浮，其勢然也。今廟堂之所廣厲，官師之所漸摩，欲挽澆醨而度之淳古之世，則莫若明學術以正人心。士有操異學者禁，肆僻說者禁，博名高而亂瞻聽者禁，使士務窮經而不至于叛經，然後統紀可一而習尚可正矣。顧取舍之柄方懸於上，若禁之于彼，售之于此，是猶民之文身向上而好之，□□人之楚語而已…
translation_en: …[to suit their?] [?] tastes, and pick up their bizarre and eccentric phrases to form their diction. When discussing the Way and virtue, they invariably invoke abstruse emptiness; when deliberating on statecraft, they invariably consult legalist techniques—while regarding the Six Classics, on the contrary, with contempt. This is the abuse of daring to rebel against the Classics. Indeed, as scholarly learning grows daily more skewed and literary style ever more decadent, its entrenchment in men's minds has not come about in a single morning or evening. Even if two gentlemen like Han Yu 韓愈 and Ouyang Xiu 歐陽修 were to emerge and strive to turn the tide in their midst, those men would remain mired in their old practices as their guiding arrows, belittle orthodox discourse as mere shifting words, and band together to disparage and secretly laugh at them. Could this be transformed and guided by empty words alone? As someone in antiquity said: "Scholars love reputation just as water flows downward; whatever those above are fond of, those below will carry to an even greater extreme." Therefore, while the common people follow their superiors according to their commands, scholars model themselves on their superiors according to their unspoken intentions. Once a single unadorned and sincere piece succeeds in the examinations, all that is superficial transforms into elegance; once a single artful and specious piece succeeds, all that is elegant transforms into superficiality—such is the natural momentum of things. Today, through the broad encouragement of the imperial court and the gradual cultivation by officials and teachers, if we wish to reverse this thin and decadent ethos and carry it back to an era of pure antiquity, nothing is better than clarifying scholarly learning in order to rectify men's minds. Among scholars, those who pursue heterodox learning should be prohibited, those who indulge in perverse doctrines should be prohibited, and those who court lofty reputations while confusing what people see and hear should be prohibited. Cause scholars to devote themselves to thoroughly mastering the Classics without going so far as to rebel against the Classics; only then can the guiding thread of orthodoxy be unified and prevailing customs be rectified. Yet the authority to select or reject presently rests above. If you prohibit such things on the one hand while rewarding them with examination success on the other, it is like when the people tattoo their bodies because their superiors are fond of it, or [forbidding?] [?] men to speak the language of Chu while doing so oneself…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
則習之見聞滋惑何以示之趨乎夫惟有
世道之責者畫法而守懸衡而較俾所好
不異於所令則煒麗之習漸袪而雅馴之
風可還矣
第五問
馬象乾
同考試官主事吳批學能博古識足匡時
同考試官編修黃批書生談邊事乃詳覈如斯亦究
心時務者
===
考試官侍讀學士申批陳諸邊利害緩急歷歷如指掌而制
馭機宜卓有遠識用世才也錄之
考試官大學士張批學子類能道古語及時事非乖剌即
迂漫可厭此策歷籌邊鎮事具有本末是留心世務者取之
古策士籌邊事者其說有三曰和曰戰曰
守而已侈薄伐之績者主於戰而戰不可
以黷也譚獻琛之頌者主於和而和不可
常恃也持衡於二者之間隨其叛服而應
之使和與戰之權在中國而不在夷狄則

古策士籌邊事者其說有三曰和曰戰曰
守而已侈薄伐之績者主於戰而戰不可
以黷也譚獻琛之頌者主於和而和不可
常恃也持衡於二者之間隨其叛服而應
之使和與戰之權在中國而不在夷狄則
punctuated:
則習之見聞滋惑，何以示之趨乎？夫惟有世道之責者，畫法而守，懸衡而較，俾所好不異於所令，則煒麗之習漸袪，而雅馴之風可還矣。

第五問

馬象乾

同考試官主事吳批：學能博古，識足匡時。
同考試官編修黃批：書生談邊事，乃詳覈如斯，亦究心時務者。
考試官侍讀學士申批：陳諸邊利害緩急，歷歷如指掌，而制馭機宜，卓有遠識，用世才也。錄之。
考試官大學士張批：學子類能道古，語及時事，非乖剌即迂漫可厭。此策歷籌邊鎮事，具有本末，是留心世務者。取之。

古策士籌邊事者，其說有三：曰和，曰戰，曰守而已。侈薄伐之績者主於戰，而戰不可以黷也；譚獻琛之頌者主於和，而和不可常恃也。持衡於二者之間，隨其叛服而應之，使和與戰之權在中國而不在夷狄，則
translation_en:
…whilst one habituates them to it [?], what they see and hear will only grow more bewildered—how then can one show them the direction to follow? Only if those who bear responsibility for the moral order of the world lay down the rules and uphold them, suspend the balance and weigh by it, ensuring that what they favor does not differ from what they command, will the habit of flashy华麗 embellishment gradually be dispelled and the ethos of refined elegance be restored.

Question Five

Ma Xiangqian 馬象乾

Comment by Associate Examiner Secretary Wu 吳: His learning encompasses antiquity, and his insight suffices to rectify the times.
Comment by Associate Examiner Compiler Huang 黃: For a scholar to discuss frontier affairs in such detailed and verified fashion shows that he too is one who earnestly applies his mind to current affairs.
Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Shen 申: He sets forth the advantages and disadvantages, the urgencies and priorities of the various frontiers as clearly as pointing to the palm of one's hand, and regarding the opportune methods of control and management, he possesses outstanding foresight—a talent useful to the world. Record it for publication.
Comment by Examiner Grand Secretary Zhang 張: Scholars are generally able to speak of antiquity, but when their words touch upon current affairs, if they are not perverse and contradictory, they are pedantically diffuse and tiresome. This policy essay successively plans out the affairs of the frontier commands, possessing both root and branch; he is one who pays heed to the affairs of the world. Select it.

Among ancient strategists who planned frontier affairs, their doctrines were three: namely peace, war, and defense—nothing more. Those who boast of the achievements of punitive expeditions advocate war, yet war cannot be waged wantonly; those who recite eulogies on presenting tribute treasures advocate peace, yet peace cannot be permanently relied upon. To hold the balance between the two, responding to them according as they rebel or submit, so that the authority over peace and war rests with China and not with the barbarians—then…

title: 萬曆五年會試錄
text:
守其最要矣是故養吾不用之力馭彼不
測之情時而和也則其恩足以懷時而戰
也則其威足以讋此制勝之遠猷禦夷之
上策也方今
聖天子威德遠被虜酋款塞願永作外藩即虞
周之世奚以加焉乃執事深憂遐慮借漢
事以策諸生圖所以善後之畫甚盛心也
愚請以漢事對夫漢興數苦虜患鴈門上
谷間蓋靡一日寧也和親之議發於婁敬
===
逮至孝文始與通關市歲往來長城下以
為常彼其時虜氛方熾而中國瘡痍之民
又靡然息肩是念用是捐細故申明約以
求安邊境漢之籌此至熟矣顧其背約棄
好敢為禍始者常在匈奴此賈誼所為發
憤流涕者也乃建武永平間當二虜分爭
之後其勢已折北不支一時謀夫扞將方
頓足攘臂爭言衛霍之事虜寇邊求合市

… defense is the most essential of all. Therefore, by cultivating our unexpended strength to control their unpredictable dispositions, when the time calls for peace, our grace is sufficient to win them over; when the time calls for war, our might is sufficient to overawe them. This is the far-reaching plan for securing victory and the supreme strategy for defending against the barbarians. At present, the august majesty and virtue of the Sacred Son of Heaven extend afar; the caitiff chieftains have knocked at the frontier passes, wishing to serve forever as an outer screen—even the eras of Yu and Zhou could not surpass this! Yet Your Excellency, with deep concern and far-sighted deliberation, borrows the affairs of the Han to pose a policy question to us students, seeking plans for managing the aftermath; this is a most magnanimous intention. I beg to reply by way of the affairs of the Han.

When the Han arose, it repeatedly suffered from the caitiff menace; in the region between Yanmen and Shanggu, there was scarcely a single day of peace. The proposal for marriage alliances (heqin) was initiated by Lou Jing; reaching the time of Emperor Xiaowen, the court first opened border markets with them, and their annual coming and going beneath the Great Wall became the norm. At that time, the caitiff threat was blazing fiercely, while within China the wounded and exhausted populace unanimously longed only to rest their weary shoulders. For this reason, the court set aside minor grievances and reaffirmed clear covenants in order to seek peace along the frontiers; the Han had calculated this most thoroughly. Yet the ones who violated covenants, abandoned good faith, and dared to initiate hostilities were always the Xiongnu—this was what caused Jia Yi to burst into indignation and shed tears.

Then, during the Jianwu (25–56) and Yongping (58–75) reigns, following the internecine split between the two caitiff factions, their power had already been broken and routed beyond recovery. At that moment, strategists and valiant generals were stamping their feet and baring their arms, vying to speak of the exploits of Wei Qing and Huo Qubing. Yet when the caitiffs raided the frontier and requested joint border markets, the court still bent its will to grant them; this was to display weakness. And when the caitiffs presented tribute of furs and horses and requested reed-organs (yu), zithers (se), …
